objectives: Connect Hebb's hypothesis, LTP/LTD, the STDP timing window, and the NMDA–Ca2+–AMPA mechanism into a conditional explanatory sequence, distinguishing empirical regularities from proposed mechanisms.
Derive the expected weight dynamics \(E[dw/dt]=Cw\) from a centered firing-rate Hebbian rule, explaining vector orientation, matrix shape, and why mean subtraction permits depression.
Use a quadratic form to prove that a covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, then use an eigenbasis to explain why the direction of greatest variance grows fastest.
Compare how synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and the BCM sliding threshold regulate overall magnitude, local normalization, and the boundary between LTP and LTD.
Distinguish unsupervised, supervised, and reward-based learning, and explain how an error, reward, or reward-prediction error can gate plasticity as a third factor.
prerequisiteBridge: Begin by treating firing rate as mean spiking intensity within a time window and synaptic weight \(w_{i}\) as the coefficient describing how input \(x_{i}\) influences postsynaptic rate h. Under a linear approximation, \(h=w^\mathrm{T} x\) is the weighted sum of the inputs. Both w and x are M×1 column vectors, whereas \(w^\mathrm{T} x\) is a scalar; this shape convention is used throughout the expected Hebbian dynamics. A rate approximation discards the exact timing of individual spikes, so it is appropriate for slower mean weight evolution but cannot replace the millisecond causal ordering represented by STDP.

Because the random input differs from trial to trial, separate a single update from its average across trials. Write the centered variable as \(x-\mu\), where \(\mu =E[x]\). Entry i,j of the covariance matrix \(C=E[(x-\mu )(x-\mu )^\mathrm{T}]\) describes whether two inputs tend to depart from their respective means in the same direction; diagonal entries are variances. Mean subtraction is essential: it includes both joint increases and joint decreases and allows the product of deviations to be negative.

The first-order differential equation \(dw/dt=aw\) has solution \(w(t)=w(0)e^{at}\): its magnitude grows exponentially for \(a>0\) and decays for \(a<0\). An eigenvector v satisfies \(Cv=\lambda v\), meaning that the matrix preserves its direction and scales only its magnitude by \(\lambda\). Any initial weight vector that can be expanded in the eigenvectors decomposes into independently growing modes, providing the mathematical entry point for analyzing Hebbian blow-up and stabilizing rules.

diagnostic.prompt: Under the standard pair-based STDP convention \(\Delta t=t_{\mathrm{post}}-t_{\mathrm{pre}}\), what are the sign of \(\Delta t\) and the usual direction of weight change when the presynaptic spike precedes the postsynaptic spike?
diagnostic.answer: \(\Delta t>0\), and the classical window commonly assigns potentiation, so \(\Delta w>0\); this is nevertheless an empirical pattern for particular synapses, states, and paired-stimulation protocols.
diagnostic.explanation: Pre-before-post timing makes glutamate release more likely to overlap with postsynaptic depolarization, promoting NMDA current and a Ca2+ signal. Bursts, neuromodulators, dendritic location, and membrane-voltage state can all reshape the window, so its sign is not a universal law.

diagnostic.prompt: If h and \(x_{i}\) are always nonnegative, why can the basic Hebbian rule \(dw_{i}/dt\propto hx_{i}\) not generate LTD? Which centered quantity can become negative?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(hx_{i}\ge 0\), the update can only vanish or increase the weight; the centered product \((h-E[h])(x_{i}-E[x_{i}])\) can be negative.
diagnostic.explanation: If the input is above its mean while the output is below its mean, or vice versa, the two deviations have opposite signs and their product lowers the weight. A centered rule learns shared fluctuations rather than shared absolute activity.

diagnostic.prompt: Given a covariance matrix C and an arbitrary vector v, why can \(v^\mathrm{T} C\) v never be less than zero?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(v^\mathrm{T} C\) \(v=E[(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu ))^2]\), the mean squared scalar projection.
diagnostic.explanation: Each sample is first projected onto v to produce a real number. Its square is nonnegative, and the expectation of nonnegative values is also nonnegative. The same argument shows that theoretical covariance eigenvalues are nonnegative.

diagnostic.prompt: For \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), starting the basic expected Hebbian dynamics at \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\), which component becomes dominant? Does the weight norm stabilize on its own?
diagnostic.answer: The first component grows as \(e^{4t/\tau }\), faster than the second component's \(e^{t/\tau }\); the direction therefore approaches the first axis, while the norm remains unbounded.
diagnostic.explanation: Hebbian dynamics can select the principal covariance direction but supplies no negative feedback on magnitude. Direction selection and norm stabilization are separate problems; the latter requires scaling, Oja-like, or BCM-like mechanisms.

modules.title: From Synaptic Timing and Receptor Mechanisms to a Firing-Rate Hebbian Rule
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a local synapse convert the timing relation between pre- and postsynaptic activity into a lasting weight change, and how can that phenomenon be abstracted into a computable rate rule?
paragraphs: Hebb's original proposal links coincident activity to stronger connectivity. Experimentally, high-frequency stimulation of the CA3-to-CA1 pathway can induce long-term potentiation (LTP), whereas a low-frequency protocol can induce long-term depression (LTD). Both describe persistent changes in synaptic efficacy after induction. Neither is the same as transient facilitation, and a single response curve cannot establish one unique molecular mechanism.

Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) makes relative timing part of the update. Let \(\Delta t=t_{\mathrm{post}}-t_{\mathrm{pre}}\). A classical pair-based window is often written as \(\Delta w=A_{+}e^{-\Delta t/\tau _{+}}\) for \(\Delta t>0\) and \(\Delta w=-A_{-}e^{\Delta t/\tau _{-}}\) for \(\Delta t<0\). The exponential terms encode weaker local coincidence at longer intervals. A_± and τ_± depend on the experimental protocol; they are not constants shared by every brain region.

The canonical mechanism is conditional: the presynaptic terminal releases glutamate; AMPA current helps depolarize the postsynaptic membrane; depolarization relieves the Mg2+ block of the NMDA pore; and NMDA-mediated Ca2+ influx converts pre/post coincidence into an intracellular signal. A shorthand account can make Mg2+ unblock sound as if presynaptic release triggered it, so the distinction must be explicit: presynaptic release provides glutamate, whereas postsynaptic depolarization relieves the block. A stronger Ca2+ signal, or one with a different time course, can favor kinase activity and AMPA insertion; another range can favor phosphatase activity and AMPA removal. The point is this conditional sequence, not a one-way description of Ca2+ as an LTP switch.

A rate model discards millisecond timing of individual spikes and retains activity strength over a window. The basic rule \(\tau _{w} dw_{i}/dt=h x_{i}\) produces only potentiation when h,\(x_{i}\ge 0\). Three covariance variants center the output, the input, or both. Each separates co-fluctuation above a variable's own baseline from merely having a large absolute value. Centering both variables is especially direct statistically because its expectation yields the input covariance.
keyPoints: LTP and LTD are experimentally observed lasting changes in efficacy; an STDP window summarizes an empirical result for a particular timing protocol.
NMDA coincidence detection requires glutamate together with postsynaptic depolarization, after which Ca2+ can influence AMPA trafficking.
A basic nonnegative Hebbian rule can only increase weights; centering activity allows negative covariance to produce depression.

derivation.title: From a Doubly Centered Local Update to Covariance Learning
derivation.setup: Let \(x\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times 1}\) and \(w\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times 1}\), with linear output \(h=w^\mathrm{T} x\). Learning is slower than neural activity, so treat w as fixed while taking the expectation over the input ensemble.

steps.title: Write the Centered Local Rule
steps.explanation: At synapse i, set \(\tau _{w} dw_{i}/dt=(h-E[h])(x_{i}-E[x_{i}])\). In vector form, \(\tau _{w} dw/dt=(x-\mu _{x})(h-E[h])\), whose right-hand side remains M×1.

steps.title: Express the Output Deviation Through the Input Deviation
steps.explanation: Because \(h=w^\mathrm{T} x\) and w is fixed within the ensemble average, \(E[h]=w^\mathrm{T} \mu _{x}\), hence \(h-E[h]=w^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu _{x})\).

steps.title: Take the Expectation and Identify the Covariance
steps.explanation: After substitution, form the outer product first and multiply w on the right: \(E[(x-\mu )(x-\mu )^\mathrm{T}]w=C_{xw}\). Thus the expected update is the action of the covariance matrix on the current weight direction.
steps.latex: \tau_w\mathbb E[\dot{\mathbf w}]=\mathbb E[(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\mathsf T}]\mathbf w=C_x\mathbf w

symbolNotes: \(C_{x}\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times M}\); \(C_{ij}\) has units \(\mathrm{input}_{i}\times \mathrm{input}_{j}\) and is dimensionless when the inputs have been standardized.
\(\tau _{w}\) is the learning time constant; w is oriented as a column vector, h is a scalar, and the transpose cannot be omitted.
derivation.unitsCheck: If both x and h are measured in Hz, the right-hand side of the unscaled rule has units \(\mathrm{Hz}^2\). A proportionality coefficient or \(\tau _{w}\) must absorb the required units so that \(dw/dt\) has units weight/time. Course equations commonly suppress this biological scale factor.
derivation.limitCheck: If the input covariance is zero, the expected update is zero. If all activities remain positive and are not centered, the rule reduces to pure growth and cannot represent anticorrelation or LTD below baseline.

workedExample.title: How Two Activity States Produce Potentiation or Depression
workedExample.problem: An input has \(\operatorname{mean} 5 \mathrm{Hz}\) and the postsynaptic output has \(\operatorname{mean} 10 \mathrm{Hz}\). Compare state A, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=14\), with state B, \(x_{i}=8\),\(h=7\), taking one update to be proportional to the product of deviations.
steps: In state A, the deviations are +3 and +4; their product is +12, so this sample drives potentiation.
In state B, the deviations are +3 and -3; their product is -9, so this sample drives depression.
With the basic product \(hx_{i}\) instead, the two states give 112 and 56. Both are positive, so the rule cannot distinguish joint elevation from one variable being high and the other low.
workedExample.result: The centered rule assigns the sign from co-fluctuation relative to baseline, not from the absolute firing-rate magnitude.
workedExample.sanityCheck: When \(x_{i}\) equals its mean exactly, its deviation is zero. No matter how large h is, that sample contributes nothing to the covariance estimate for this synapse.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is a classical STDP window not interchangeable with a firing-rate covariance rule?
selfCheck.answer: STDP preserves millisecond relative timing between pre- and postsynaptic spikes, whereas a covariance rule averages activity fluctuations over a longer window. They can be related under specific statistical and timescale assumptions, but they use different state variables, experimental protocols, and levels of mechanistic interpretation.

pitfalls: Treating the NMDA–Ca2+ sequence as the sole mechanism at every synapse while ignoring neuromodulation, dendritic voltage, and burst context.
Saying only “fire together, wire together” without specifying baseline centering, the sign of the update, or the learning timescale.

modules.title: Covariance Geometry, the PSD Proof, and Hebbian Eigenmode Blow-Up
modules.guidingQuestion: Why do covariance eigenvectors provide the natural coordinates for Hebbian learning, and why does the largest eigenvalue cause both directional selection and unstable growth?
paragraphs: The expected dynamics \(\tau _{w} E[dw/dt]=Cw\) form a linear dynamical system. An eigenvector \(v_{k}\) of C satisfies \(Cv_{k}=\lambda _{k}v_{k}\), so if w lies along \(v_{k}\), the update remains in that direction and changes only its magnitude. For a symmetric covariance matrix, the eigenvectors can be chosen as an orthogonal basis, allowing any initial w to be written as \(\sum _k a_{k}v_{k}\).

Covariance is symmetric because \(C_{ij}=E[(x_{i}-\mu _{i})(x_{j}-\mu _{j})]\), and exchanging the two scalar factors leaves their product unchanged. It is also positive semidefinite (PSD): for every v, the quadratic form \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) is the expected square of the projection \(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu )\). PSD does not require every off-diagonal entry to be positive. Anticorrelated variables may have negative covariance while the full quadratic form remains nonnegative.

In the eigenbasis, each coefficient obeys \(\tau _{w} da_{k}/dt=\lambda _{k}a_{k}\), with solution \(a_{k}(t)=a_{k}(0)e^{\lambda _{k}t/\tau _{w}}\). The mode with the largest \(\lambda\) grows faster than the others, so the normalized direction approaches the principal eigenvector. This produces the formal link to PCA while exposing the defect of basic Hebbian learning: because PSD eigenvalues are nonnegative, no existing component is actively reduced by these expected dynamics.

A direction approaching PC1 is not the same as a weight vector converging to a stable PC1 solution. Under the basic rule the norm keeps increasing until the assumptions of a linear neuron, stationary statistics, and a fixed learning rate fail. A stable PCA-like solution can be discussed only after normalization or competition controls magnitude. A nonlinear output, nonstationary input, or several similar eigenvalues can alter both convergence and the resulting direction.
keyPoints: The central evidence that covariance is symmetric PSD is \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv=E[(v^\mathrm{T}(x-\mu ))^2]\ge 0\).
The eigenbasis decomposes coupled weight dynamics into independent exponential modes, with \(\lambda _{k}\) setting each mode's growth rate.
Selection of a principal direction does not imply norm stability; Hebbian learning equals PCA only under additional assumptions.

derivation.title: PSD, Nonnegative Eigenvalues, and the Eigenmode Solution
derivation.setup: Assume \(C=E[(x-\mu )(x-\mu )^\mathrm{T}]\) has finite second moments and is a real symmetric M×M matrix.

steps.title: Rewrite the Quadratic Form as a Square
steps.explanation: Insert the definition of C into \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) and use linearity of expectation to move the vectors into the sample expression. The two scalar factors multiply to the square of the same projection.
steps.latex: \mathbf v^{\mathsf T}C\mathbf v=\mathbb E[(\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu))^2]\ge 0

steps.title: Infer the Sign of an Eigenvalue
steps.explanation: If \(Cv=\lambda v\) with \(v\ne 0\), then \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv=\lambda v^\mathrm{T}v\). Since the denominator \(v^\mathrm{T}v=||v||^2>0\), \(\lambda =(v^\mathrm{T}Cv)/||v||^2\ge 0\).

steps.title: Expand and Solve Each Coefficient
steps.explanation: Write \(w=\sum _ka_{k}v_{k}\) and substitute it into \(\tau _{w} dw/dt=Cw\). Coefficients of the orthogonal eigenvectors can be matched term by term, yielding independent first-order ODEs.

symbolNotes: \(\lambda _{k}\) has the same units as covariance; in a normalized model, the learning-rate scale commonly absorbs those units so the exponent is dimensionless.
\(a_{k}\) is the coordinate of the weight vector along the population-wide statistical direction \(v_{k}\), not an individual synapse.
derivation.unitsCheck: The exponent \(\lambda _{k}t/\tau _{w}\) must be dimensionless. If \(\lambda\) has units \(\mathrm{input}^2\), the learning-rate coefficient in the complete model must have units reciprocal \(\mathrm{input}^2\).
derivation.limitCheck: For \(\lambda _{k}=0\), that mode's coefficient remains at its initial value. If the two largest eigenvalues are equal, there is no unique principal direction; the outcome depends on initialization and noise.

workedExample.title: Growth Rates and Direction for a Two-Dimensional Covariance
workedExample.problem: Let \(C=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(\tau _{w}=1 \mathrm{s}\), and \(w(0)=(1,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute the two components and their ratio at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\).
steps: The eigenvectors are the coordinate axes \(e_{1}\),\(e_{2}\), with eigenvalues 4 and 1, respectively.
The ratio \(w_{1}/w_{2}=e^3\approx 20.09\), so the direction is already close to the first axis; yet the norm is about 54.67, far above its initial value \(\sqrt 2\).
workedExample.result: The direction of greatest variance rapidly dominates while the total weight magnitude explodes; both consequences arise from the same positive-feedback dynamics.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If C is replaced by the zero matrix, both components remain 1. If its diagonal entries are exchanged, the ultimately dominant axis is exchanged as well.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does a negative off-diagonal covariance entry not violate positive semidefiniteness?
selfCheck.answer: Positive semidefiniteness constrains the variance \(v^\mathrm{T}Cv\) along every complete direction, not each matrix entry separately. Two variables can be anticorrelated, giving \(C_{ij}<0\), while every linear combination still has a variance equal to an expected square.

pitfalls: Interpreting an eigenvector as one particular neuron or synapse; it is a direction in the full input or weight space.
Noticing that the principal direction dominates but overlooking that every component still grows exponentially, and therefore claiming incorrectly that basic Hebbian learning is stable.

modules.title: Stabilizing Rules and Third-Factor Learning
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a system retain Hebbian feature selection while preventing weight blow-up, and how can learning be restricted to appropriate moments when a target or reward is required?
paragraphs: Synaptic scaling slowly rescales a group of synapses together so that total weight or postsynaptic activity returns to a target range. It can preserve the relative weight pattern, but it requires some cell-wide measurement. Restoring the norm to a fixed value after each Hebbian change still allows the direction to rotate toward the principal covariance eigenvector while preventing unbounded amplitude growth.

Oja's rule incorporates normalization into a local approximation: \(dw/dt\propto hx-h^2w\). The first term is Hebbian correlation; the second grows with output energy and the current weight, creating weight-dependent decay. For centered, linear, stationary input, the expected fixed point can align with the principal eigenvector while retaining a finite norm. That result belongs to these simplifying assumptions, not to every variant of Oja's rule.

The BCM rule changes the sign of plasticity using a postsynaptic sliding threshold, for example \(dw_{i}/dt\propto h x_{i}(h-\theta )\), while \(\theta\) adapts to recent \(h^2\). With \(h<\theta\), the same presynaptic activity tends toward LTD; with \(h>\theta\), it tends toward LTP. Sustained higher activity raises \(\theta\) and makes potentiation harder to trigger. Unlike Oja's explicit weight decay, BCM creates competition and stability through an activity-dependent sign switch.

Unsupervised learning uses only input and neural activity to discover statistical structure. Supervised learning additionally requires a target-output error, whereas reward learning selects advantageous behavior through reward or deviation from expected reward. A three-factor rule multiplies pre-activity, post-activity, and a modulatory third signal. That factor controls when or in which direction a local eligibility trace is consolidated, but it need not always be dopamine and is not equivalent to a backpropagated gradient assigned precisely to every weight.
keyPoints: Scaling rescales synapses globally; Oja's rule combines a Hebbian term with local weight-dependent decay; BCM uses a dynamic postsynaptic threshold.
The connection between Oja's rule and PCA requires centered, linear, stationary input and a suitable learning rate.
Three-factor learning supplements pre/post coactivity with an error, reward, or contextual gate.

derivation.title: How an Oja Fixed Point Selects Direction and Controls Norm
derivation.setup: Use a centered linear neuron \(h=w^\mathrm{T} x\), let \(C=E[xx^\mathrm{T}]\), and write the expected Oja dynamics as \(E[dw/dt]=\eta (Cw-(w^\mathrm{T}Cw)w)\).

steps.title: Evaluate the Two Expectations
steps.explanation: \(E[hx]=E[xx^\mathrm{T}]w=Cw\), while \(E[h^2]=E[w^\mathrm{T}xx^\mathrm{T}w]=w^\mathrm{T}Cw\), the output variance along the current direction.
steps.latex: \mathbb E[h\mathbf x]=C\mathbf w,\qquad \mathbb E[h^2]=\mathbf w^{\mathsf T}C\mathbf w

steps.title: Substitute an Eigenvector Candidate
steps.explanation: If \(w=a v_{k}\) and \(||v_{k}||=1\), then \(Cw=a\lambda _{k}v_{k}\) and \(w^\mathrm{T}Cw=a^2\lambda _{k}\). The dynamics stay along \(v_{k}\), and the amplitude satisfies da/dt=ηλ_ka(1-a^2).

steps.title: Identify the Finite Fixed Amplitudes
steps.explanation: For \(\lambda _{k}>0\), \(a=\pm 1\) are finite fixed points. The amplitude grows when \(0<a<1\) and decays when \(a>1\). Competition among directions makes the mode with the largest \(\lambda\) stably dominant for common initializations.

symbolNotes: \(\eta\) is the learning rate and must be small enough for noisy online updates to approximate the expected ODE.
The fixed norm of 1 here follows from the scaling convention of the rule; other parameterizations can impose a different target norm.
derivation.unitsCheck: The terms \(h^2w\) and hx must have the same units. A biological rule requires proportionality constants or normalized variables to make them match; the abstract equation usually absorbs those scales into \(\eta\).
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\lambda _{k}=0\), that direction has no statistical drive. If the input is nonstationary, conclusions based on a fixed C and a fixed principal component no longer apply.

workedExample.title: How the BCM Threshold Reverses the Sign of Change at One Synapse
workedExample.problem: Let \(x_{i}=2\) and use \(x_{i}\) \(h(h-\theta )\) as the core update. Set \(\theta =5\), compare \(h=3\) with \(h=8\), and then explain how sustained high activity changes \(\theta\).
steps: For \(h=3\), \(2\times 3\times (3-5)=-12\), so the update is depressive.
For \(h=8\), \(2\times 8\times (8-5)=48\), so the update is potentiating.
If \(h^2\) remains high over time, the sliding-threshold dynamics raise \(\theta\), making the same future h less likely to cross the potentiation threshold.
workedExample.result: BCM uses the postsynaptic operating point to determine the sign of plasticity and uses slow threshold feedback to counteract runaway growth from persistently high activity.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The instantaneous update is zero when \(h=\theta\) or \(x_{i}=0\); changing presynaptic activity alone cannot substitute for crossing the postsynaptic threshold.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is it inadequate to reduce a reward-based three-factor rule to “Hebbian learning multiplied by dopamine”?
selfCheck.answer: The third factor may encode reward, reward-prediction error, an error signal, context, or another neuromodulatory gate. Its timing, receptors, eligibility trace, and specificity for the target weight all affect learning, so dopamine is only one candidate implementation in some systems.

pitfalls: Treating synaptic scaling, Oja's rule, and BCM as interchangeable names for normalization, despite their different measured variables and feedback locations.
Taking a formal resemblance to a three-factor rule as proof of a complete biological mechanism for backpropagation or a reward circuit.

objectives: Define a supervised-learning problem in terms of its dataset, architecture, loss, and learning rule, and distinguish the target support of classification from that of regression.
Use a first-order Taylor expansion to explain why the gradient is the locally steepest ascent direction and why a step along the negative gradient reduces squared loss.
Derive the linear-regression gradient, its Hebbian-like and stabilizing components, and the normal equation step by step, including how to handle a singular design matrix.
Explain why a deep linear network has a linear input-output map even though its multilayer factorization produces nonlinear and generally nonconvex optimization dynamics.

Derive the backpropagated error recurrence and each layer's weight gradient by tracking shapes, while treating backpropagation as a training algorithm rather than an established neurobiological mechanism.
prerequisiteBridge: A supervised dataset contains P paired examples \((x_\mu ,y_\mu )\). Here \(x_\mu\) is an N×1 feature vector. If each sample is placed in one column of X, then \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times P}\). Scalar-regression targets form \(y\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\), and the prediction is \(X^\mathrm{T} w\). In classification, y is commonly a discrete label or one-hot vector; in regression it may be continuous.

A gradient collects all partial derivatives and has the same shape as its parameter. For a scalar function \(L(w)\), a small perturbation \(\Delta w\) gives the first-order change \(\Delta L\approx \nabla L^\mathrm{T}\Delta w\). A dot product equals the product of vector lengths and the cosine of their angle. With step length fixed, choosing \(\Delta w\) parallel to \(-\nabla L\) makes this linear approximation as negative as possible.

The chain rule differentiates compositions: if \(y=f(z)\) and \(z=g(x)\), then \(dy/dx=(dy/dz)(dz/dx)\). A multilayer network repeatedly applies this rule, but matrix shapes determine where transposes and outer products appear. The derivative of a square is \(d(e^2)/de=2e\). For \(z=Wx\), entry \(W_{ij}\) affects only \(z_{i}\), with a derivative proportional to \(x_{j}\).

diagnostic.prompt: What must a supervised-learning algorithm specify separately, and why is “use a neural network” not a complete specification?
diagnostic.answer: It must specify the architecture or representation, the loss or objective, the optimization or learning rule, and the dataset's input-target pairing.
diagnostic.explanation: The architecture determines which mappings can be represented, the loss defines error, and the learning rule determines how parameters change. The same architecture can be trained with different losses, and the same loss can be optimized in different ways.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(\nabla L=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\) and a local step is limited to length 0.1, which direction minimizes the linear term in the Taylor expansion?
diagnostic.explanation: The gradient norm is 5. For a fixed step length, the dot product is smallest at an angle of 180°, so use the unit negative gradient. Standard gradient descent instead lets \(\eta ||\nabla L||\) determine the step length.

diagnostic.prompt: With \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times P}\) and \(w\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}\), what are the shapes of the least-squares prediction, residual, and gradient?
diagnostic.answer: Both the prediction \(X^\mathrm{T}w\) and residual \(y-X^\mathrm{T}w\) are P×1. Under this lecture's convention \(L=||y-X^\mathrm{T}w||^{2}/P\), the gradient is \(-(2/P)X(y-X^\mathrm{T}w)\), with shape N×1. The factor 2 disappears only if the loss includes 1/2.
diagnostic.explanation: The factor 2 comes from differentiating the square. Left-multiplying the residual by X aggregates the errors from P samples back into N feature coordinates. When only direction matters, one may write that the gradient is proportional to -Xr; with an equality sign, however, 2/P cannot be omitted.

diagnostic.prompt: Let \(W^1\in \mathbb{R}^{4\times 3}\), \(W^2\in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 4}\), and \(x\in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 1}\). If output error \(\delta ^2\in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 1}\), what are the shapes of the hidden error and \(\partial L/\partial W^1\)?
diagnostic.answer: \(\delta ^1=(W^2)^\mathrm{T}\delta ^2\odot \phi '\) is \(4\times 1\), and \(\partial L/\partial W^1=\delta ^1x^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4\times 3\).
diagnostic.explanation: The transposed weight matrix maps error from output space back into hidden coordinates. An outer product then combines postsynaptic error with presynaptic activation to produce the gradient for every connection.

modules.title: The Components of Supervised Learning and Gradient Descent
modules.guidingQuestion: How is a prediction task formulated as an optimizable mathematical problem, and how does local loss geometry imply a parameter update?
paragraphs: Supervised learning supplies input-target pairs. In handwritten-digit recognition, x is an image and y is a discrete digit label, making the task classification. In optic-flow estimation, x may be two adjacent frames and y a continuous motion vector at each location, making it regression. Both require a clear account of how training examples are sampled and whether test examples follow the same distribution.

The architecture specifies the prediction function. A multilayer network can be written \(z^{(0)}=x\), \(h^{(\ell )}=W^{(\ell -1)}z^{(\ell -1)}\), \(z^{(\ell )}=\phi (h^{(\ell )})\), and finally \(\hat{y}=g(W^{(L)}z^{(L)})\). If layer ℓ contains \(N_\ell\) units, then \(W^{(\ell -1)}\in \mathbb{R}^{N_\ell \times N_{\ell -1}}\). Writing every shape exposes most transpose errors before the derivation begins.

A loss compresses the discrepancy between prediction and target into a scalar. Squared error is common for regression and cross-entropy for classification; choosing a loss embeds assumptions about noise and task priorities. An optimization rule then determines how W changes. Conflating architecture, loss, and learning rule makes it impossible to identify whether a performance change arose from representation, objective, or optimizer.

In a parameter plane, squared-loss contours are ellipses. The gradient is perpendicular to a contour and points locally uphill. A first-order Taylor approximation is reliable only for a sufficiently small step, so the learning rate \(\eta\) must be neither so large that it jumps across the valley nor so small that training stalls. The negative gradient is a local descent direction; it does not take a deep network to a global optimum in one step.
keyPoints: The dataset supplies the evidence defining the problem, the architecture defines the hypothesis class, the loss defines error, and the optimizer defines the search path.
A gradient has the same shape as its parameter and points in the locally steepest ascent direction; gradient descent applies the negative sign.
The Taylor argument is local. With an excessively large learning rate, the loss can rise instead of fall.

derivation.title: Deriving Gradient Descent from a Taylor Expansion and Computing a Single-Sample Linear Gradient
derivation.setup: Use scalar prediction \(\hat{y}=w^\mathrm{T}x\), loss \(L(w)=1/2(y-\hat{y})^2\), and parameter step \(\Delta w\).

steps.title: Write the First-Order Change in Loss
steps.explanation: Near the current w, the dot product of the gradient and a small step controls the loss change; second- and higher-order terms are smaller when the step is sufficiently short.
steps.latex: L(\mathbf w+\Delta\mathbf w)\approx L(\mathbf w)+\nabla L(\mathbf w)^{\mathsf T}\Delta\mathbf w

steps.title: Choose a Local Descent Direction
steps.explanation: Set \(\Delta w=-\eta \nabla L\). The linear term becomes \(-\eta ||\nabla L||^2\le 0\), with \(\eta >0\) setting the step size.

steps.title: Apply the Chain Rule to Squared Error
steps.explanation: Let \(e=y-w^\mathrm{T}x\). Then \(\partial L/\partial e=e\) and \(\partial e/\partial w=-x\), so the gradient is -ex and the update is \(+\eta ex\). A positive error therefore raises the prediction along x.

symbolNotes: \(\eta\) has units parameter^2/loss so that \(\eta \nabla L\) has parameter units; after normalization it is often treated simply as a numerical hyperparameter.
For a batch loss, the gradient is the mean of the P sample gradients, not the product obtained by averaging x and y first.
derivation.unitsCheck: If y and ŷ are measured in deg/s while x is dimensionless, the gradient has units \((\mathrm{deg}/s)^2\) per weight; \(\eta\) must convert the update back to weight units.
derivation.limitCheck: The gradient vanishes when the residual \(e=0\) or \(x=0\). If \(\eta\) is too large, the neglected second-order term can cause the loss to increase.

workedExample.title: A Gradient Step Computed by Hand
workedExample.problem: Let \(x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), \(y=5\), \(w=(0,0)^\mathrm{T}\), \(L=1/2(y-w^\mathrm{T}x)^2\), and \(\eta =0.1\). Compute the update and the new loss.
steps: Initially the prediction is 0 and residual \(e=5\), so \(\mathrm{gradient}=-ex=(-5,-10)^\mathrm{T}\).
The update gives \(w_{\mathrm{new}}=w-\eta \mathrm{gradient}=(0.5,1.0)^\mathrm{T}\).
The new prediction is \(0.5+2=2.5\), and the new loss is \(1/2(5-2.5)^2=3.125\); the initial loss was 12.5.
workedExample.result: The negative-gradient step moves the prediction toward the target and reduces the loss by a factor of four.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Both the gradient and w are \(2\times 1\). If the update's negative sign is mistakenly removed, w becomes (-0.5,-1), \(\mathrm{prediction}=-2.5\), and the loss increases to 28.125.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is the statement “the gradient points toward the minimum” inaccurate?
selfCheck.answer: The gradient points in the locally steepest ascent direction at the current point; its negative is the local descent direction. It uses only first-order information at that location and does not directly identify a distant global minimum.

pitfalls: Classifying a task as classification or regression only by the model's name instead of examining target support and loss.
Turning the negative gradient's local descent guarantee into a global guarantee for every learning rate and every nonconvex network.

modules.title: Linear Regression: Gradient Decomposition, the Normal Equation, and Deep Linear Factorization
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does linear regression offer both an interpretable local learning rule and a closed-form solution, while optimization becomes more complicated after linear layers are stacked?
paragraphs: Adopt the source notes' orientation: every column of \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times P}\) is a sample, \(w\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times 1}\), \(y\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\), and the prediction is \(X^\mathrm{T}w\). The batch loss is \(L=||y-X^\mathrm{T}w||^2/P\). Its gradient aggregates the correlation between each feature and the residual, so the update contains the data-dependent Hebbian-like term Xy.

Expanding the gradient gives \(\nabla L=(2/P)(XX^\mathrm{T}w-Xy)\). Thus \(-\nabla L\) contains \(+(2\eta /P)\)Xy and \(-(2\eta /P)XX^\mathrm{T}w\). The first term writes input-target coactivity into the weights; the second grows with the current weights and input covariance, providing stabilization. Its form resembles biological Hebbian learning, but a target y, batch access, and signed error are not ordinary local coactivity.

Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) yields the normal equation \(XX^\mathrm{T} \hat{w}=Xy\). If \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is invertible, \(\hat{w}=(XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}\)Xy. Redundant features or \(P<N\) can make the matrix singular, so its inverse must not be forced. The pseudoinverse selects a minimum-norm solution, while ridge regression replaces \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) with \(XX^\mathrm{T}+\lambda I\), exchanging a small bias for numerical stability.

If every activation in a deep linear network is the identity, its overall map \(M=W^{(L)}\cdots W^{(0)}\) remains linear: \(\hat{y}=Mx\). Yet many layer factorizations represent the same M, and the loss contains products of individual layer weights. Consequently, the parameter landscape and learning dynamics are nonlinear. A linear represented function does not make the optimization problem ordinary convex regression.
keyPoints: A least-squares update decomposes into input-target correlation and weight-dependent covariance stabilization.
A closed form requires a stated orientation for X and invertibility; use a pseudoinverse or regularization when the system is singular.
The function class of a deep linear network is still linear, but factorized parameters create nonconvexity and nonunique scaling.

derivation.title: The Batch Least-Squares Gradient and Normal Equation
derivation.setup: Define residual \(r=y-X^\mathrm{T}w\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\) and loss \(L=(1/P)r^\mathrm{T}r\). To retain the source notes' scaling, do not include 1/2.

steps.title: Expand the Scalar Loss
steps.explanation: Expand the quadratic as \(y^\mathrm{T}y-2y^\mathrm{T}X^\mathrm{T}w+w^\mathrm{T}XX^\mathrm{T}w\). The first term is independent of w.
steps.latex: L=\frac1P(\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y-2\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf w+\mathbf w^{\mathsf T}XX^{\mathsf T}\mathbf w)

steps.title: Differentiate Term by Term
steps.explanation: The linear term contributes -2Xy/P; since \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is symmetric, the quadratic term contributes \(2XX^\mathrm{T}w/P\).

steps.title: Set the Gradient to Zero
steps.explanation: At a stationary point, \(XX^\mathrm{T} \hat{w}=Xy\). Squared loss is a convex quadratic; if \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is positive definite, this point is the unique minimum.

symbolNotes: \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is an N×N feature-covariance-scale matrix, whereas Xy is an N×1 feature-target correlation vector.
With the samples-as-rows convention, the formula becomes \((X^\mathrm{T}X)^{-1}X^\mathrm{T}y\); the two conventions must not be mixed.
derivation.unitsCheck: The quantities \(XX^\mathrm{T}w\) and Xy have matching feature×target scales. Large differences among feature units worsen conditioning and sensitivity to the learning rate, so standardization is often needed.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(XX^\mathrm{T}\) is singular, the inverse does not exist. Gradient descent may still reach an interpolating solution, but initialization, optimizer, and regularization determine which one it selects.

workedExample.title: A Closed-Form Fit with Two Features and Two Samples
workedExample.problem: Let \(X=[[1,0],[0,2]]\), so its columns are \((1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \((0,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and let targets \(y=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\). Find \(\hat{w}\).
steps: \(XX^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)\), and \(Xy=(3,8)^\mathrm{T}\).
\((XX^\mathrm{T})^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/4)\), hence \(\hat{w}=(3,2)^\mathrm{T}\).
The predictions \(X^\mathrm{T}\hat{w}=(3,4)^\mathrm{T}\) exactly match the targets, so the residual is zero.
workedExample.result: Because the sample value of feature 2 is 2, a weight of only 2 predicts target 4; the closed form respects feature scaling.
workedExample.sanityCheck: In this example, incorrectly using \(X^\mathrm{T}X\) also happens to give a diagonal matrix and can conceal an orientation bug. With a general nonsquare X, the shapes reveal the error immediately.

selfCheck.prompt: Why can training every layer of a deep linear network not be treated as ordinary convex linear regression, even though the overall mapping is linear?
selfCheck.answer: The product \(W^L\cdots W^0\) defines a linear mapping, but it is a multilinear product of the component layer parameters. Scale and factorization are nonunique, and updates to different layers depend on one another, so optimization in parameter space is generally nonconvex.

pitfalls: Applying a closed-form formula without declaring whether samples are columns or rows, thereby misplacing transposes and dimensions.
Directly inverting a singular or ill-conditioned matrix instead of considering a pseudoinverse, ridge regularization, and feature scaling.

modules.title: Backpropagation: Layerwise Chain Rules, Error Coordinates, and Weight Gradients
modules.guidingQuestion: How is an output error re-expressed, through local derivatives, as the sensitivity of each layer's preactivation and then converted into a gradient with the same shape as each weight matrix?
paragraphs: The forward pass stores each preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}=W^{(\ell -1)}z^{(\ell -1)}\) and activation \(z^{(\ell )}=\phi (h^{(\ell )})\). Backpropagation does not physically send the target backward through the network; it computes derivatives of the scalar loss with respect to intermediate variables. Define \(\delta ^{(\ell )}=\partial L/\partial h^{(\ell )}\), whose dimension equals the number of units in that layer.

Looking backward from layer ℓ+1, \(h^{(\ell +1)}=W^{(\ell )}z^{(\ell )}\). One hidden activation influences every downstream preactivation, so the sensitivity is first multiplied by \((W^{(\ell )})^\mathrm{T}\) to aggregate downstream error and then multiplied elementwise by \(\phi '(h^{(\ell )})\). The transpose follows from the coordinate mapping; it is not optional notation.

Each weight \(W^{(\ell -1)}_{ij}\) contributes presynaptic activation \(z^{(\ell -1)}_j\) to postsynaptic preactivation \(h^{(\ell )}_i\). Therefore \(\partial L/\partial W_{ij}=\delta _{i} z_{j}\), and the complete matrix gradient is the outer product \(\delta ^{(\ell )}(z^{(\ell -1)})^\mathrm{T}\). Batch training averages these outer products.

The derivative of the nonlinear activation determines whether error can pass through a unit. A saturated sigmoid has a very small derivative and can cause vanishing gradients, whereas large weights can cause exploding gradients. ReLU has derivative 1 in its positive region and 0 in its negative region, which can also produce inactive units. Backpropagation is an exact chain-rule algorithm. Its outer-product form can be compared with biological three-factor rules, but weight transport, a global target, and update timing remain mechanistic differences.
keyPoints: \(\delta\) denotes the derivative of loss with respect to a preactivation, not a directly observed biological firing error.
The hidden-error recurrence contains the transpose of the downstream weights and the derivative of the local activation.
A weight gradient is the outer product of postsynaptic sensitivity and presynaptic activation.

derivation.title: Backpropagation Recurrence in a Two-Layer Network
derivation.setup: Let \(h^1=W^0x\), \(z^1=\phi (h^1)\), \(h^2=W^1z^1\), and \(\mathrm{prediction}=h^2\); the loss may be any differentiable scalar.

steps.title: Define the Output Sensitivity
steps.explanation: First compute \(\delta ^2=\partial L/\partial h^2\) directly from the loss. For squared error \(L=1/2||y-h^2||^2\), \(\delta ^2=h^2-y\).

steps.title: Propagate Sensitivity to the Hidden Preactivation
steps.explanation: The chain rule first passes through the linear map to give \((W^1)^\mathrm{T}\delta ^2\) and then through the elementwise nonlinearity to give the hidden \(\delta\).

steps.title: Form the Two Weight Gradients
steps.explanation: Each matrix gradient is the outer product of that layer's postsynaptic \(\delta\) and its incoming activation, so its shape matches automatically.
steps.latex: \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(1)}}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(2)}(\mathbf z^{(1)})^{\mathsf T},\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{(0)}}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(1)}\mathbf x^{\mathsf T}

symbolNotes: If \(W^0\) is H×N and \(W^1\) is O×H, then \(\delta ^1\) is H×1 and \(\delta ^2\) is O×1; the two gradients are H×N and O×H, respectively.
⊙ denotes elementwise multiplication. Replacing it with matrix multiplication changes both the shape and the numerical meaning.
derivation.unitsCheck: The units of \(\delta\) are loss/preactivation. Multiplication by a presynaptic activation gives loss/weight, as required by the definition of a gradient.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\phi '=0\) for a hidden unit, that unit transmits no gradient to upstream weights for the current sample. This does not mean the unit is permanently useless, although sustained inactivity blocks learning.

workedExample.title: Tracing One Backpropagation Path by Shape
steps: The hidden activation is \(z^1=W^0x=(1,2)^\mathrm{T}\), and prediction \(\hat{y}=(1,-1)\cdot (1,2)=-1\).
\(\delta ^2=\hat{y}-y=-1\), and \(\delta ^1=(W^1)^\mathrm{T}\delta ^2=(-1,1)^\mathrm{T}\).
\(\partial L/\partial W^1=\delta ^2(z^1)^\mathrm{T}=(-1,-2)\), while \(\partial L/\partial W^0=\delta ^1x^\mathrm{T}=[[-1,-2],[1,2]]\).
workedExample.result: The two gradient shapes are \(1\times 2\) and \(2\times 2\), and every entry can be verified from its local outer product.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A small increase in \(W^1_1\) raises ŷ. The current residual is -1, so raising ŷ moves it toward target 0; accordingly, the gradient with respect to \(W^1_1\) is negative and the negative-gradient update increases that weight.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does the backpropagated error recurrence use the transpose of the downstream weight matrix?
selfCheck.answer: The forward map W carries hidden coordinates into downstream coordinates. The chain rule must aggregate downstream scalar sensitivities back into each hidden coordinate, which is exactly the reverse Jacobian product \(W^\mathrm{T}\delta\); its shape also returns from the downstream dimension to the hidden dimension.

pitfalls: Describing \(\delta\) as an error molecule that literally propagates backward through biological neurons, without separating a computed derivative from its possible implementation.
Memorizing the recurrence without labeling h, z, \(\delta\), and W shapes at every layer, which invites errors at transposes and elementwise derivatives.

objectives: Use the course-level photoreceptor–RGC–V1–MT/IT/LIP diagram to explain the visual hierarchy while separating anatomical pathways, receptive-field computations, and functional labels.
Explain every stage of the LNP model—linear filter, static nonlinearity, and conditional Poisson output—and why early vision is commonly modeled in terms of contrast rather than raw luminance.
Construct ON and OFF Difference-of-Gaussians receptive fields through spatial convolution and predict the response signs for a uniform field, a center spot, and surround illumination.

Decompose a Gabor kernel into its Gaussian envelope, carrier frequency, orientation, and phase; then explain how the subsequent static nonlinearity introduces thresholding and saturation in V1 simple-cell orientation tuning.
Extend receptive fields into space-time, distinguish separable from nonseparable kernels, and infer direction selectivity from slope in an x-t diagram.
prerequisiteBridge: A receptive field is not merely an area of the screen; it is a relation between a stimulus pattern and a neural response. A linear spatial receptive field \(K(x,y)\) assigns a positive or negative weight to each location. Multiplying stimulus contrast \(s(x,y)\) by K everywhere and summing gives scalar drive L. Positive weights prefer bright contrast and negative weights prefer dark contrast, although the exact sign depends on the ON/OFF convention.

Define contrast as \(s=(I-I_{0})/I_{0}\), where I is local luminance and \(I_{0}\) is the adapted mean luminance. Division by \(I_{0}\) makes the same relative change comparable across background levels. A Poisson model converts a nonnegative rate r and time window T into the count distribution n~\(\operatorname{Poisson}(rT)\). It describes conditional variability and does not imply that real spikes are perfectly independent.

Only elementary trigonometry is needed for a two-dimensional rotation: \(x'=x \cos\theta +y \sin\theta\) and \(y'=y \cos\theta -x \sin\theta\). In the carrier \(\cos(kx'+\phi )\), k controls spatial angular frequency and \(\phi\) controls phase. After time is added, each stimulus history is an x-y-t volume. A moving edge traces an oblique line in the x-t plane whose slope is set by velocity.

diagnostic.prompt: For \(I_{0}=100\) and local \(I=120\), what is the contrast? If \(I_{0}=200\) and local \(I=220\), how does contrast change even though the raw increment is the same?
diagnostic.answer: The first contrast is 0.2; the second is 0.1.
diagnostic.explanation: Contrast measures relative change. The same 20-unit luminance increment is proportionally smaller on the brighter background, so an early-vision model should not compare raw differences alone.

diagnostic.prompt: If an ON-center kernel has zero total integral, what should its linear response be when uniform positive contrast covers both center and surround?
diagnostic.answer: Approximately zero, because the positive center contribution cancels the negative surround contribution.
diagnostic.explanation: A zero-integral center-surround filter removes the common luminance component while preserving spatial differences. A real cell may deviate from exactly zero because of imperfect balance, nonlinearity, and adaptation.

diagnostic.prompt: If k increases in a Gabor kernel while the Gaussian envelope stays fixed, which aspect of tuning changes?
diagnostic.answer: The carrier's spatial frequency increases and its ON/OFF lobes become more closely spaced; rotation \(\theta\) sets the preferred orientation.
diagnostic.explanation: k determines phase change per unit distance along x', \(\theta\) determines the carrier coordinate's direction, and \(\phi\) translates the light and dark lobes.

diagnostic.prompt: Why can a fully separable kernel \(K(x,t)=K_{x}(x)K_{t}(t)\) generally not distinguish two moving edges with equal speeds and opposite directions using only its linear response?
diagnostic.answer: Its spatial preference has the same shape and position at every time lag, so it contains no tilted x-t structure encoding the order of locations.
diagnostic.explanation: Direction selectivity requires coupling spatial position to temporal delay. In a nonseparable kernel the preferred position changes with lag, matching a trajectory in one direction while rejecting the reverse trajectory.

modules.title: Visual Hierarchy, the LNP Model, and Center-Surround Computation
modules.guidingQuestion: How does the visual system turn a luminance image into local contrast features and connect a receptive field to spikes through a minimal probabilistic model?
paragraphs: The source notes place photoreceptors, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), V1, MT, IT, and LIP on a hierarchy diagram. The retina first encodes local contrast; V1 emphasizes local structure such as orientation; MT and the dorsal stream are associated with motion and action-relevant variables; IT and the ventral stream with object features; and LIP often with decision-related representations. This course-level computational map does not imply exclusively one-way feedforward information flow.

Along the hierarchy, classical receptive fields generally become larger, the selected features more complex, and history dependence and context stronger. Higher-level cells may also become more invariant to position, phase, or local detail. Feature selectivity asks which stimulus pattern changes the response; a receptive field additionally asks which positions and time lags matter. A single heat-map color cannot capture both questions.

The LNP model has three ordered stages: linear, nonlinear, and Poisson. The linear stage \(L=K*s\) measures the match between a stimulus and a receptive-field template. The nonlinearity \(r=F(L)\) rectifies, thresholds, or saturates the drive to produce a plausible rate. Finally, n~\(\operatorname{Poisson}(rT)\) describes count variability conditional on the stimulus. LNP is descriptive; it does not claim that each stage occupies a separate anatomical box.

A Difference of Gaussians (DoG) often approximates an RGC center-surround receptive field. An ON-center filter subtracts a broad negative Gaussian from a narrow positive one; an OFF-center filter reverses every sign. If their integrals nearly balance, a uniform field cancels while center-surround differences are amplified. Threshold-linear rectification \([L]_{+}=\max(L,0)\) then separates ON and OFF drives into nonnegative feature maps.
keyPoints: The visual hierarchy mixes anatomy with computational abstraction; a region label is not an exclusive function.
An LNP linear drive may have either sign, the nonlinearity makes rate nonnegative, and a conditional distribution then generates spike count.
A DoG center-surround filter suppresses common luminance and highlights local contrast and edges.

derivation.title: From Contrast and Convolution to an ON-Center DoG
derivation.setup: Let \(r^2=x^2+y^2\) and define the normalized 2D Gaussian \(G_\sigma (r)=(2\pi \sigma ^2)^{-1}\exp[-r^2/(2\sigma ^2)]\), whose total integral is 1.

steps.title: Normalize Luminance First
steps.explanation: Use adaptation level \(I_{0}\) as baseline and define dimensionless contrast. When \(I=I_{0}\), \(s=0\); luminance above baseline is positive and luminance below it is negative.

steps.title: Define a Translated Receptive-Field Drive
steps.explanation: With cell center \((x_{0},y_{0})\) as reference, multiply the kernel by the stimulus at every position and integrate. Differences in the kernel arguments express the same receptive-field shape at different center locations.

steps.title: Construct Center-Surround and Test a Uniform Field
steps.explanation: Let \(K=A G_{\sigma _{c}}-B G_{\sigma _{s}}\), with \(\sigma _{s}>\sigma _{c}\). If \(A=B\), the integral of K is zero, so uniform contrast \(s_{0}\) gives \(L=s_{0}\int K=0\).

symbolNotes: \(\sigma _{c}\) and \(\sigma _{s}\) have units of spatial distance. A and B set integrated center and surround strength, not merely peak height.
K must have units such that K×area×contrast yields a linear drive. For discrete pixels, the integral becomes a sum that includes the pixel-area factor.
derivation.unitsCheck: Contrast is dimensionless. If x,y are measured in degrees of visual angle, a normalized Gaussian has units degree^{-2}, and integration leaves L with the drive units of A and B.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(\sigma _{s}=\sigma _{c}\) and \(A=B\), the entire kernel is zero. If the surround is broad but B is not scaled for its area, comparing peak heights misrepresents total inhibitory strength.

workedExample.title: Predicting Signs in a Discrete Three-Position Center-Surround Filter
workedExample.problem: Use \(K=(-0.5,1,-0.5)\) for the left surround, center, and right surround. Compare stimuli \(s_{A}=(0,1,0)\) and \(s_{B}=(1,1,1)\), then rectify.
steps: \(L_{B}=-0.5+1-0.5=0\); the balanced kernel cancels uniform contrast.
With the OFF-center kernel -K, stimulus A gives -1 and therefore 0 after [L]_+.
workedExample.result: The ON-center filter has positive drive for a local bright spot and no linear drive for a uniform bright field; the OFF-center channel is suppressed by that same bright spot.
workedExample.sanityCheck: A zero sum of kernel weights is exactly the discrete condition for uniform cancellation. A nonzero sum leaves a residual response to a uniform field.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is “ON cells prefer light and OFF cells prefer dark” an incomplete account of a center-surround receptive field?
selfCheck.answer: The response depends on contrast location and surround context. A bright spot in an ON center can excite, whereas a bright surround can cancel it. A balanced kernel may not respond to the same global luminance, so both polarity and spatial pattern must be specified.

pitfalls: Treating a receptive field as a purely geometric boundary without defining its internal positive and negative weights, time lags, and response measure.
Comparing Gaussian centers and surrounds only by peak height while ignoring width, integrated strength, and the kernel sign convention.

modules.title: Feature Maps, Gabor Simple Cells, and Orientation Tuning
modules.guidingQuestion: How can one localized sinusoidal filter jointly select position, orientation, spatial frequency, and phase, and how do its responses form a feature map?
paragraphs: Convolving one kernel over all retinal locations produces a feature map. Each map pixel records how well the surrounding image patch matches the feature template; it is not the original image intensity. ON and OFF kernels yield two polarity-specific maps, and rectification retains positive drive for each filter's preferred polarity. This resembles shared filters in convolutional neural networks mathematically, but it does not make biological wiring, learning rules, or boundary treatment identical.

V1 simple-cell receptive fields often contain alternating elongated ON and OFF lobes. A Gabor kernel uses a Gaussian envelope to localize position and size and a cosine carrier to create the alternating lobes. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinates, k controls spatial frequency, and \(\phi\) controls phase. Orientation tuning arises because positive contributions add when an edge aligns with the lobes, whereas an orthogonal edge straddles positive and negative regions and cancels.

Changing \(\theta\) rotates the preferred orientation. Changing \(\phi\) translates the bright-dark lobe pattern along the carrier direction without changing orientation or frequency. Increasing k packs more lobes into each unit distance. Collapsing all three parameters into a single “direction” label prevents predictions about phase reversal or different bar widths.

A rectifying, saturating nonlinearity can turn linear Gabor drive into firing rate, for example \(r=r_{\mathrm{max}}[L]_{+}^2/(\alpha ^2+[L]_{+}^2)\). The response rises for small positive L, approaches \(r_{\mathrm{max}}\) for large L, and clips negative L. Localized sinusoidal analysis is mathematically related to wavelets and JPEG because all represent images with local scale-orientation components; this does not mean cortex implements the same codec.
keyPoints: Each location in a feature map stores a filter response, not a copy of the input image.
For a Gabor filter, the envelope sets localization, \(\theta\) sets orientation, k sets frequency, and \(\phi\) sets phase.
The nonlinearity determines sign handling, threshold, and saturation, so a single linear kernel can produce different tuning amplitudes.

derivation.title: How a Rotated Gabor Filter Produces Orientation-Selective Drive
derivation.setup: Start with coordinates (x,y) and use \(\theta\) to define carrier-aligned coordinates. Different Gaussian widths \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\) create an elongated envelope.

steps.title: Rotate the Coordinate System
steps.explanation: x' runs along the preferred carrier normal and y' is perpendicular to it. Rotation preserves distance and stimulus content; it changes only the coordinate basis.

steps.title: Write the Localized Carrier
steps.explanation: The Gaussian restricts the filter to a finite region, while the cosine generates alternating positive and negative lobes within it. Normalization can be chosen for the application.

steps.title: Explain the Tuning
steps.explanation: For a grating with matching k,\(\theta\),\(\phi\), regions of equal sign overlap and the inner product is large. A phase difference of \(\pi\) reverses the linear response; rectification can therefore make the two firing responses different.

symbolNotes: k is measured in radians per spatial distance, and cycles per degree equals \(k/(2\pi )\). Whether \(\theta\) names the grating's bar orientation or differs from it by 90° depends on whether orientation is defined by the wave-vector normal or the bar axis.
\(\phi\) is in radians and changes ON/OFF lobe alignment. \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\) use the same spatial units as x,y.
derivation.unitsCheck: Both kx' and \(\phi\) must be dimensionless, so k has units inverse distance. The exponential argument \(x'^2/\sigma _{x}^2\) is dimensionless as well.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\sigma _{x}\),\(\sigma _{y}\to \infty\), localization is lost. As \(k\to 0\), the carrier approaches a constant and the kernel resembles a Gaussian blob rather than an oriented alternating filter.

workedExample.title: Simple-Cell Responses at One Orientation and Different Phases
workedExample.problem: Idealize the linear drive to a matching grating as \(L=A \cos(\phi _{s}-\phi _{K})\), with \(A=10\). Compare phase differences 0, \(\pi /2\), and \(\pi\) using \(r=[L]_{+}\).
steps: At difference 0, \(L=10cos0=10\) and \(r=10\).
At difference \(\pi /2\), \(L=10\cos(\pi /2)=0\) and \(r=0\).
At difference \(\pi\), \(L=10\cos\pi =-10\) and rectification gives \(r=0\).
workedExample.result: Simple-cell firing depends on both orientation/frequency matching and alignment of the light-dark phase.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Without rectification, the response at phase \(\pi\) is -10 rather than no response; nonnegativity of firing rate comes from the nonlinear stage.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does changing Gabor phase \(\phi\) not change preferred orientation \(\theta\)?
selfCheck.answer: \(\phi\) translates positive and negative lobes along a fixed carrier axis and determines whether a bright or dark edge aligns with the filter. \(\theta\) rotates the coordinate system and determines which edge or grating direction aligns with the elongated lobes.

pitfalls: Confusing the grating wave-vector direction with bar orientation without noting that they usually differ by 90°.
Treating rectification or saturation as part of the linear receptive field rather than distinguishing linear drive L from firing rate r.

modules.title: Spatiotemporal Receptive Fields and Motion as Space-Time Orientation
modules.guidingQuestion: Why must direction selectivity link “where” with “how long ago” instead of using independent spatial and temporal filters?
paragraphs: After time is included, the linear drive integrates past stimulus history: \(K(x',y',\tau )\) multiplies \(s(x-x',y-y',t-\tau )\), with \(\tau \ge 0\) denoting look-back time. Temporal lobes may be biphasic so that sustained components of a static image cancel. Because center and surround can have different time courses, an RGC receptive field is commonly nonseparable.

Every time slice of a separable kernel \(K(x,y,t)=K_{s}(x,y)K_{t}(t)\) has the same spatial pattern, differing only by a scalar amplitude. It can express a fixed-location feature that excites and then inhibits, but it cannot move the preferred location. In a nonseparable kernel, positive and negative lobes shift with lag, binding spatial position to temporal order.

A vertical edge moving rightward at velocity v satisfies \(x(t)=x_{0}+vt\). In an x-t diagram it is an oblique line of slope \(dx/dt=v\). If the positive lobes of a receptive field lie along the same line, the edge traverses every positive zone in sequence and produces a large inner product. An edge moving the other way follows the opposite slope and encounters mismatched positive and negative zones.

A rightward-motion receptive field has precisely this tilted pattern. Direction selectivity can also be built from multiple filters, quadratic motion energy, or recurrence, so a tilted linear receptive field is a testable minimal description. Eye movements, coordinate transformations, and finite display refresh alter the stimulus trajectory; experiments must state the reference frame.
keyPoints: Spatiotemporal convolution uses past stimulus history, so the orientation of the time-lag axis must be explicit.
A separable kernel's spatial profile does not move with lag; a tilted nonseparable kernel can encode the sign of velocity.
Motion is an orientation in the x-t plane, and velocity corresponds to trajectory slope.

derivation.title: The Matching Condition for a Moving Edge and a Tilted Receptive Field
derivation.setup: Ignore y and concentrate moving-edge contrast at \(x=x_{0}+vt\). Let a receptive-field ridge be concentrated at \(x=x_{c}-v\tau\), where \(\tau\) is a past lag.

steps.title: Write the Edge Position in the History
steps.explanation: Looking back by lag \(\tau\) from current time t places the edge at time \(t-\tau\) and position \(x_{0}+v(t-\tau )=x_{0}+vt-v\tau\), so its history trajectory has slope -v with respect to lag.

steps.title: Align the Edge with the Receptive-Field Ridge
steps.explanation: If the receptive-field ridge follows \(x=x_{c}-v\tau\) and \(x_{c}=x_{0}+vt\), the edge falls on the positive ridge at every lag, so all contributions add with the same sign.

steps.title: Reverse Direction to Produce a Mismatch
steps.explanation: Changing velocity to -v gives history trajectory \(x_{0}-vt+v\tau\). Its slope reverses, it no longer overlaps the original ridge, and it may cross inhibitory lobes.

symbolNotes: \(\tau\) is a nonnegative look-back time, not absolute clock time. If a receptive-field plot places the past above rather than below, the visible slope sign changes with the plotting convention.
v has units spatial distance/time, such as degree/s; x and receptive-field position must use the same spatial reference frame.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(v\tau\) has distance units and can be added to x. The spatiotemporal integral also includes dx \(d\tau\), so kernel normalization must preserve the drive units.
derivation.limitCheck: At \(v=0\) the ridge is untilted and selects a static feature. With an extremely short temporal window, opposite-direction trajectories have not separated enough and direction discrimination weakens.

workedExample.title: Matching a Discrete Three-Frame Trajectory
workedExample.problem: Across frames at times t-2,t-1,t, a rightward edge occupies positions 0,1,2. Put the receptive field's positive positions at 0,1,2 for the corresponding lags. Award +1 for a match and 0 otherwise; compare this sequence with leftward positions 2,1,0.
steps: The rightward sequence matches at all three lags, giving total linear drive \(1+1+1=3\).
The leftward sequence matches only at middle position 1; the other two frames mismatch, so total drive is 1.
With threshold 2, the rightward response passes and the leftward response is clipped to 0.
workedExample.result: The same three positions produce different responses when their temporal order differs; direction selectivity arises from a space-time conjunction.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the three frames are averaged without order, both sequences contain positions \({0,1,2}\), and the distinction disappears. Temporal order is therefore indispensable.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does a biphasic temporal kernel not automatically guarantee direction selectivity?
selfCheck.answer: If the kernel still factors into a fixed spatial profile and a temporal waveform, it only reweights one spatial feature over time and never pairs distinct locations with particular lags. Direction selectivity requires space-time nonseparability or an equivalent multichannel nonlinear computation.

pitfalls: Mixing time lag with absolute time, thereby flipping the receptive field on the temporal axis and reversing the inferred preferred direction.
Explaining motion tuning from a single-frame spatial receptive field without checking the joint pattern across positions and lags.

objectives: Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component.
Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis.
Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance.
Starting from \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), derive the proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance.
Recover a static nonlinearity with the small-bin Poisson approximation and diagnose STA failure caused by multiple features, an even nonlinearity, colored stimuli, or insufficient data.
prerequisiteBridge: An LNP model first takes the inner product between stimulus-history vector \(s_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\) and filter \(K\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\), giving \(L_{t}=K^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\), and then maps \(L_{t}\) through nonlinearity F to a rate. P may flatten pixels together with x, y, and several past time lags into one index. Every experimental time bin supplies one column \(s_{t}\), so the design matrix is \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\).

Least squares chooses K so that \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) approximates measured response h. Its gradient is \(-S(h-S^\mathrm{T}K)/T\); setting it to zero gives \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\). The Hessian \(SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) describes loss curvature along filter directions. If one stimulus direction is scarcely sampled, its curvature is small and the filter estimate becomes highly noise-sensitive.

Here white noise means that distinct pixel/time dimensions are approximately zero-mean, uncorrelated, and equal-variance, so the large-sample covariance approaches \(\sigma _{s}^2I\). With sufficiently small bins, spike count \(k_{t}\) is usually 0 or 1 and \(P(k_{t}=1|L_{t})\approx \Delta tF(L_{t})\). The STA averages stimulus vectors preceding spike bins, all aligned to the same lags.

diagnostic.prompt: What does column t of \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\) represent, and why is K^TS_{:t} a scalar?
diagnostic.answer: It is the stimulus history preceding time t, flattened in a fixed lag order. K and that column are both P-dimensional, so their inner product is one linear drive.
diagnostic.explanation: Each time bin is one high-dimensional regression example. Placing time in rows while retaining the original formulas misaligns the orientations of K, S, and the response.

diagnostic.prompt: What experimental problem is indicated by a small eigenvalue of the least-squares Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\)?
diagnostic.answer: The stimulus varies little along that eigenvector direction, so loss curvature is weak and the data constrain that filter component poorly.
diagnostic.explanation: Many K values displaced along that direction give almost identical predictions, leaving the estimate dominated by measurement noise or regularization. Identifiability improves only by adding stimulus variation in that direction.

diagnostic.prompt: Why are loss contours nearly circular, rather than tilted ellipses, for large-sample equal-variance white noise?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), all orthogonal filter directions have equal curvature and cross-terms are nearly zero.
diagnostic.explanation: The identity matrix favors no coordinate direction. Finite samples still create off-diagonal fluctuations, so circularity is an approximation rather than exact geometry in every experiment.

diagnostic.prompt: A neuron fires strongly when \(|K^\mathrm{T}s|\) is large and responds identically to positive and negative projections. Why can its linear STA be nearly zero?
diagnostic.answer: Stimuli resembling +K and -K both precede spikes, and the two groups cancel in their vector average.
diagnostic.explanation: A zero first moment does not imply an absence of stimulus dependence. Spike-triggered covariance can reveal increased variance along K, and an energy model can represent this even response.

modules.title: White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations
modules.guidingQuestion: Given a complete stimulus movie and spike times, how can the stimulus history before each spike be converted into a dataset for estimating a filter?
paragraphs: System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. The standard protocol in the source notes presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first.

The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation.

Continuous notation writes \(L(t)=\int dx'\) dy' dt' \(K(x',y',t')s(x',y',t-t')\). After discretization, combine (x,y,t') into index p to obtain \(L_{t}=\sum _pK_{p}S_{pt}\). Matrix notation is \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\). All three forms express the same inner product. Matrix form is convenient for least squares, whereas continuous form shows spatial location and causal lag directly.

Each column of S is an entire stimulus history, not just the current frame; the p entries of K follow the same flattening order. Reversing the lag index flips the estimated kernel in time. A white-noise protocol matters not because the pattern merely looks random, but because different dimensions have nearly diagonal sample covariance on a common scale, reducing estimator bias and uneven uncertainty.
keyPoints: An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient.
Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) are alternative representations of the same calculation.
The defining benefit of white noise is covariance isotropy, not an arbitrarily generated noisy picture.

derivation.title: Discretizing Spatiotemporal Convolution as \(S^\mathrm{T}K\)
derivation.setup: Use \(N_{x}\times N_{y}\) pixels and \(N_\tau\) causal lags, for total dimension \(P=N_{x}N_{y}N_\tau\); the experiment contains T usable time bins.

steps.title: Define a Compound Index
steps.explanation: Assign a unique p to every \((x_{i},y_{j},\tau _{q})\), write \(K(x_{i},y_{j},\tau _{q})\) as \(K_{p}\), and write the past stimulus \(s(x_{i},y_{j},t-\tau _{q})\) corresponding to time t as \(S_{pt}\).

steps.title: Replace the Integral with a Grid-Volume-Weighted Sum
steps.explanation: Spatial and temporal discretization introduces the factor \(\Delta x\Delta y\Delta \tau\). Absorbing it into \(K_{p}\) leaves an ordinary dot product.

steps.title: Stack All Time Bins into a Vector
steps.explanation: \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is T×P; multiplying it by P×1 vector K produces T×1 vector L, with each row reproducing one time-bin inner product.

symbolNotes: In this lecture T denotes sample count but is also commonly used for physical time. Within matrix shapes it means the number of bins, and explanations should keep the meanings distinct.
The time coordinate of K is look-back lag: \(\tau =0\) is the current or most recent bin, and positive \(\tau\) refers to earlier stimuli.
derivation.unitsCheck: If continuous K has units drive/(contrast·area·time), multiplying by contrast and dx dy \(d\tau\) gives drive. If discrete K absorbs grid volume, its numerical units depend on binning.
derivation.limitCheck: A frame rate that is too low aliases fast temporal structure. A history window that is too short truncates the kernel; one that is too long increases P and reduces statistical power per dimension.

workedExample.title: Matrix Prediction with Two Pixels and Four Time Bins
workedExample.problem: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry.
steps: At t1 the stimulus is (1,1), so \(L_{1}=2\times 1+1\times 1=3\); at t2 it is (-1,1), so \(L_{2}=-2+1=-1\).
Therefore \(L=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). The first pixel has the larger weight, so changing its coordinate affects the drive more strongly.
workedExample.result: One matrix multiplication computes the filter projections for all four time bins while preserving the pairing with each stimulus column.
workedExample.sanityCheck: S is \(2\times 4\) and \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4\times 2\); multiplication by \(2\times 1\) K must yield \(4\times 1\). A 2-dimensional result signals that the orientation has been reversed.

selfCheck.prompt: Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs?
selfCheck.answer: Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure.

pitfalls: Flattening the stimulus without recording pixel and lag order, so the resulting vector cannot be reshaped correctly into a receptive field.
Calling a stimulus white merely because it looks random, without checking its mean, variance, cross-correlations, and finite-sample covariance.

modules.title: Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does stimulus covariance control uncertainty in a filter estimate, and how does white noise place different feature directions on a common scale?
paragraphs: First consider a linear neuron \(h_{t}\approx K^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\), where h may be a measured firing-rate estimate. Mean-squared loss averages prediction error over T bins. Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) gives the normal equation \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\): stimulus covariance scale times the filter equals stimulus-response cross-correlation. Identifiability depends on whether S spans the relevant directions.

For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially.

In ideal Gaussian white stimulation, every \(S_{pt}\) has zero mean and variance \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and different p dimensions are uncorrelated. At large T, \((SS^\mathrm{T})_{pq}=\sum _tS_{pt}S_{qt}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2\delta _{pq}\). Consequently \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), the loss contours are nearly circular, and every filter dimension has equal curvature.

A finite dataset never has covariance exactly equal to the identity: off-diagonal sample covariances fluctuate around zero. Unequal pixel variances produce a diagonal but anisotropic H. With colored stimuli, correlations in H cause raw cross-correlation to mix the true filter with the stimulus spectrum. One must then apply the covariance inverse explicitly, whiten the stimulus, or fit a regularized likelihood model.
keyPoints: The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation.
A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction.
White-noise isotropy is a large-sample approximation; colored stimuli require covariance correction.

derivation.title: The Normal Equation and an Isotropic Hessian
derivation.setup: Define \(L(K)=(1/2T)||h-S^\mathrm{T}K||^2\), with \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\) and \(h\in \mathbb{R}^{T\times 1}\).

steps.title: Compute the Gradient
steps.explanation: For residual \(r=h-S^\mathrm{T}K\), derivatives of prediction along the filter coordinates are supplied by S, so the gradient is -S times the residual.

steps.title: Compute the Estimate and Hessian
steps.explanation: Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) yields \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\). Differentiating the gradient once more gives \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\).

steps.title: Insert the White Covariance
