steps.explanation: For independent, equal-variance dimensions, off-diagonal sample sums approach zero and diagonal sums approach \(T\sigma _{s}^2\), so the inverse is approximately \((T\sigma _{s}^2)^{-1}I\).

symbolNotes: H is a P×P curvature matrix; it is neither neural-response covariance nor spike-triggered covariance.
\(\delta _{pq}\) is the Kronecker delta: it equals 1 for \(p=q\) and 0 otherwise, encoding ideal white covariance.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has units stimulus^2 and Sh has units stimulus×response. The resulting estimate therefore has units response/stimulus, as required for linear-filter gain.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(T\le P\) or stimulus dimensions are linearly dependent, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) may be singular and the inverse expression cannot be used directly.

workedExample.title: Recovering a Known Filter from a White Design
workedExample.problem: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares.
steps: \(SS^\mathrm{T}=[[4,0],[0,4]]=4I\), showing that the two stimulus dimensions have isotropic sample covariance.
\(Sh=(8,4)^\mathrm{T}\); for example, its first entry is \(1\times 3+(-1)\times (-1)+1\times 1+(-1)\times (-3)=8\).
\(\hat{K}=(4I)^{-1}(8,4)^\mathrm{T}=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), exactly recovering the true filter.
workedExample.result: For orthogonal equal-variance stimuli, the covariance inverse supplies only a common rescaling, so the direction of the cross-correlation is the filter direction.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the second stimulus row is replaced by a copy of the first, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\operatorname{rank} 1\). Only the sum of the two filter weights affects prediction, so the weights cannot be identified separately.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably?
selfCheck.answer: Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially.

pitfalls: Interpreting a circular loss contour as a circular receptive field; the contour describes curvature in parameter space, not spatial shape.
Using the white-noise approximation without the large-T, equal-variance, and independence assumptions.

modules.title: From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics
modules.guidingQuestion: Under which scaling and probabilistic assumptions does the stimulus average before spikes point along a linear filter, and what kinds of selectivity can this average cancel completely?
paragraphs: The data contain spike counts \(k_{t}\) rather than a continuous rate \(h_{t}\). Choose bin width \(\Delta t\) small enough that \(k_{t}\in {0,1}\) usually holds and define rate estimate \(h_{t}=k_{t}/\Delta t\). Then Sh=(1/Δt)Σ_{t:k_t=1}\(s_{t}\), the sum of spike-triggered stimulus vectors scaled by bin width.

Because \(STA=(1/n_{sp})\sum _{spikes}s_{t}\), a white design gives \(\hat{K}\approx [n_{sp}/(T\sigma _{s}^2\Delta t)]STA\). STA and K point in the same direction, but absolute amplitude depends on spike count, recording duration, stimulus variance, and bin width. Comparing raw STA amplitudes across cells or conditions can therefore mistake a firing-rate change for a filter-gain change.

After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test.

STA succeeds when one linear dimension dominates, the stimulus distribution is suitable, and spike count is adequate. Colored stimulation biases its direction; non-Gaussian input breaks the simple proportionality; multiple relevant dimensions collapse into one average; an even nonlinearity \(F(L)=F(-L)\) cancels +K and -K ensembles; and history dependence or adaptation contaminates the stimulus filter. Thus \(STA=0\) is not evidence for “no receptive field.”
keyPoints: The proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and STA contains \(n_{sp}\), T, \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and \(\Delta t\); their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude.
Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width.
An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero.

derivation.title: STA Proportionality with All Scale Factors Retained
derivation.setup: Assume white stimulation \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), bin counts \(k_{t}\in {0,1}\), rate estimate \(h_{t}=k_{t}/\Delta t\), and \(n_{sp}\) spike bins.

steps.title: Rewrite Response Cross-Correlation as a Spike Sum
steps.explanation: Bins with \(k_{t}=0\) contribute nothing; bins with \(k_{t}=1\) retain stimulus vector \(s_{t}\) and carry scale \(1/\Delta t\).

steps.title: Introduce the Definition of STA
steps.explanation: The spike sum equals spike count times the mean spike-triggered stimulus.

steps.title: Substitute the Least-Squares Estimate
steps.explanation: The covariance inverse contributes the common factor \(1/(T\sigma _{s}^2)\), yielding the proportionality between filter and STA.

symbolNotes: \(n_{sp}/T\Delta t\) is the mean firing rate, so the proportionality factor can also be written mean \(\mathrm{rate}/\sigma _{s}^2\).
STA entries have stimulus units. \(\hat{K}\) as a rate filter is additionally divided by stimulus variance, so their gain units differ.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(n_{sp}/(T\Delta t)\) has units 1/time; dividing by \(\sigma _{s}^2\) and multiplying by stimulus gives rate/stimulus, as required for a linear rate filter.
derivation.limitCheck: If bins are too wide, \(k_{t}\) can exceed 1 and the Bernoulli simplification fails. With too few spikes, STA variance is large even when the expectation relation holds.

workedExample.title: How an Even Nonlinearity Makes the STA Vanish
workedExample.problem: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance.
steps: The total spike probability is \((0.4+0.1+0.4)/3=0.3\). Bayes' rule gives \(P(s=-1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\), \(P(s=0|\mathrm{spike})=1/9\), and \(P(s=+1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\).
The positive and negative endpoints have equal conditional weight, so \(STA=E[s|\mathrm{spike}]=(-1)(4/9)+0+(+1)(4/9)=0\).
The spike-triggered second moment is \(E[s^2|\mathrm{spike}]=(4/9)+(4/9)=8/9\). Because the conditional mean is zero, this is also the spike-triggered variance.
The original stimulus has zero mean and variance \(E[s^2]=2/3\). Spike-triggered variance increases by \(8/9-2/3=2/9\), revealing a preference for large |s|.
workedExample.result: The STA is zero, yet spike-triggered variance rises from 2/3 to 8/9. STC or a quadratic model can detect the relevant direction hidden by symmetric averaging over signs.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The three conditional probabilities sum to 1. If the spike probabilities at ±1 are changed to equal that at \(s=0\), the spike-triggered distribution returns to the prior and the variance difference becomes zero.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts?
selfCheck.answer: Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there.

pitfalls: Comparing raw STA amplitudes across conditions without correcting for spike rate, stimulus variance, duration, and bin width.
Reading \(STA=0\) as proof that a neuron is not stimulus-selective while ignoring even nonlinearities and multiple-feature coding.

objectives: Explain why one STA cannot describe an H1-like or complex-cell-like response driven by multiple features, and use spike-triggered covariance eigenvectors to find stimulus directions whose variance changes.
Define the response distribution, linear predictor, and link function of a GLM, including the relation between the canonical parameter and the mean.
Write the log likelihoods for Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli probability models and explain the supports enforced by identity, log, and logit links.
Strictly separate Poisson counts, small-bin Bernoulli spike/no-spike observations, and logistic classification so their likelihoods and interpretations are not conflated.
Reconstruct the stimulus, self-history, and coupling filters of a retinal population GLM, and explain why fitted coupling provides conditional prediction rather than proof of a direct synapse.
prerequisiteBridge: STA compares the mean stimulus preceding spikes; STC compares its covariance. For centered s, \(C=E[(s-\mu )(s-\mu )^\mathrm{T}]\). If \(\Delta C=C_{\mathrm{spike}}-C_{\mathrm{stim}}\) has a positive eigenvalue along an eigenvector, variance in that direction is larger before spikes; a negative eigenvalue means values along that direction occupy a narrower range.

A likelihood multiplies the probabilities of the observed data conditional on parameters. The log likelihood converts this product into a sum, simplifying computation and optimization. A GLM does not require the response mean to be linear in x. It first forms \(\eta =x^\mathrm{T}\beta\), and link g maps conditional \(\operatorname{mean} m=E[y|x]\) to \(\eta\): \(g(m)=\eta\).

A Poisson variable supports nonnegative integer counts and has \(\operatorname{mean} \lambda >0\). A Bernoulli variable takes only 0 or 1 and has probability \(\operatorname{mean} q\). The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) guarantees a positive rate; the logit link \(\log[q/(1-q)]=\eta\) gives \(q=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\eta )\). Neural-history covariates must contain only spikes preceding the current bin, never future information.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\), what are the two eigenvalues of \(\Delta C\), and what does each mean?
diagnostic.answer: The eigenvalues are 3 and -0.75. Variance before spikes increases in the first direction and decreases in the second.
diagnostic.explanation: STC measures conditional covariance relative to raw stimulus covariance. Both positive and negative changes may reveal relevant dimensions, so keeping only the largest positive eigenvalue is unjustified.

diagnostic.prompt: Which part of a GLM is linear? Is the mean response of \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) linear?
diagnostic.answer: The predictor \(\eta =X\beta\) is linear. Through the inverse log link, the Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^\eta\) and is nonlinear in the predictor.
diagnostic.explanation: The distribution and link determine mean support and curvature. Treating a GLM as ordinary linear regression would incorrectly permit a negative mean count.

diagnostic.prompt: What mean count does \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\) predict for \(\eta =\log 2\)? What probability does a Bernoulli-logit model predict for \(\eta =0\)?
diagnostic.answer: The Poisson mean is \(\lambda =e^{\log 2}=2\); the Bernoulli probability is \(q=1/(1+e^0)=0.5\).
diagnostic.explanation: The two inverse links map any real \(\eta\) into a positive real mean and a probability in (0,1), respectively. Enforcing this support is central to link selection.

diagnostic.prompt: If the coupling filter from neuron j to neuron i has a positive coefficient in a retinal GLM, does that prove a direct excitatory connection from j to i?
diagnostic.answer: No. It says only that, conditional on the included covariates, past spikes of j improve the prediction of i's conditional rate.
diagnostic.explanation: Shared input, unobserved cells, stimulus-model mismatch, and common network state can all produce fitted coupling. Establishing a causal synapse requires perturbation or a stronger identification design.

modules.title: Multiple Relevant Features and Spike-Triggered Covariance
modules.guidingQuestion: When a neuron responds to both signs of a projection or to several directions, how can features be recovered from the shape, rather than the mean, of the pre-spike stimulus distribution?
paragraphs: The source notes use the blowfly H1 neuron, whose stimulus \(s(t)=v(t)\) is image velocity rather than a two-dimensional light pattern. The response may depend on projections through several temporal filters \(K_{1}\cdots K_{n}\) followed by a multidimensional nonlinearity F. Thus stimulus-vector coordinates are defined by the question: they may be pixels, velocity history, past spikes, or other measured covariates.

If the nonlinearity is symmetric for +K and -K, the spike-triggered mean cancels. If the response depends on several relevant filters, one STA supplies at most one mean direction. It may consistently point toward one linear combination but cannot recover the full relevant subspace. Symmetry cancellation and dimensional limitation are distinct and should not both be dismissed as a noisy or unstable average. STC computes \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) and compares it with \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\). Eigenvectors of \(\Delta C\) give directions of altered variance, and eigenvalue signs show whether variance grew or shrank.

A positive eigenvalue means that the spike-conditioned ensemble is broader along that feature direction, as when a large projection magnitude triggers spikes. A negative eigenvalue means that spikes require the projection to lie in a narrower range. An eigenvector's sign is arbitrary—v and -v are the same axis—so response sign must be inferred from the multidimensional nonlinearity.

For white stimulation \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\approx \sigma ^2I\), so \(\Delta C\) can be analyzed directly. Colored stimulation allows intrinsically high-variance input directions to dominate even when irrelevant to the neuron. One should whiten first or solve \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) \(v=\lambda  C_{\mathrm{stim}} v\). STC remains sensitive to finite spike count, high dimension, and non-Gaussian input, requiring a null distribution, regularization, and held-out validation.
keyPoints: STC finds spike-conditioned changes in variance and can reveal dimensions that symmetry hides from the STA.
Both positive and negative covariance changes are informative; an eigenvector's sign is not an excitation sign.
Colored stimuli require whitening or a generalized-eigenvalue correction relative to \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\).

derivation.title: From a Covariance Difference to Relevant Axes
derivation.setup: Let the raw stimulus mean be \(\mu _{s}\) and the spike-triggered \(\operatorname{mean} \mu _{sp}\); center each ensemble around its own mean to obtain \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\).

steps.title: Define the Covariance Change
steps.explanation: Both covariance matrices must use the same coordinate system. Their difference is symmetric.

steps.title: Write Directional Variance Change as a Quadratic Form
steps.explanation: For a unit vector v, the difference between projection variances is \(v^\mathrm{T}\Delta Cv\), directly comparing spike-conditioned spread with baseline spread.
steps.latex: \Delta\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}s)=\mathbf v^{\mathsf T}\Delta C\mathbf v

steps.title: Find the Extrema by Eigendecomposition
steps.explanation: Under the constraint \(||v||=1\), extrema of the Rayleigh quotient occur at eigenvectors of \(\Delta C\); their eigenvalues are the variance changes along those axes.

symbolNotes: Both \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}\) are P×P. When sample count is much smaller than P, their estimates are rank-deficient.
A generalized eigenvalue \(\lambda\) describes a relative variance ratio and has a different numerical scale from an eigenvalue of \(\Delta C\).
derivation.unitsCheck: Covariance and \(\Delta C\) have units stimulus^2, as do their eigenvalues. In normalized or whitened space they can be interpreted as dimensionless relative changes.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=C_{\mathrm{stim}}\), the second moment does not change and STC reveals no feature; the neuron may still depend on higher-order statistics.

workedExample.title: Positive and Negative Directions in Two-Dimensional STC
workedExample.problem: Let \(C_{\mathrm{stim}}=I\) and \(C_{\mathrm{spike}}=\operatorname{diag}(4,0.25)\). Find \(\Delta C\) and its eigenvectors, then interpret them.
steps: \(\Delta C=\operatorname{diag}(3,-0.75)\). It is already diagonal, with eigenvectors \(e_{1}=(1,0)^\mathrm{T}\) and \(e_{2}=(0,1)^\mathrm{T}\).
Along \(e_{1}\), spike-conditioned variance rises from 1 to 4, a change of +3, suggesting that large \(|s_{1}|\) is associated with spiking.
Along \(e_{2}\), variance falls from 1 to 0.25, a change of -0.75, suggesting that spiking favors \(s_{2}\) within a narrow range.
workedExample.result: One neuron can simultaneously require a large magnitude in one projection and constrain another projection; one STA cannot express both conditions.
workedExample.sanityCheck: \(\operatorname{trace} \Delta C=2.25\) is the total variance change, but the trace alone erases the axis-specific combination of one positive and one negative change.

selfCheck.prompt: Why cannot the sign of an STC eigenvector say whether a stimulus is excitatory or inhibitory?
selfCheck.answer: Covariance describes an unoriented axis. v and -v have identical squared projections and covariance. To learn how projection sign affects rate, fit or inspect the nonlinearity along that axis.

pitfalls: Selecting the largest eigenvector of \(\Delta C\) under colored stimulation and mistaking the stimulus's own high variance for a neural feature.
Reporting only positive eigenvalues and missing directions in which the spike-conditioned ensemble narrows.

modules.title: The Three GLM Components and Gaussian and Poisson Likelihoods
modules.guidingQuestion: How can the same linear covariates model a continuous response or spike count, and how does the probability model determine the objective?
paragraphs: A GLM has three components: response distribution \(p(y|\theta )\), linear predictor \(\eta =X\beta\), and link \(g(m)=\eta\) connecting \(\eta\) with conditional \(\operatorname{mean} m\). The exponential-family canonical form \(p(y|\theta )=\exp[y\theta +H(y)-D(\theta )]\) separates the data term, base measure, and log-partition function. D normalizes the distribution and determines its mean and variance.

For a unit-variance Gaussian model with identity link, \(m=\eta =x^\mathrm{T}\beta\). The β-dependent part of the log likelihood is \(-1/2\Sigma (y-m)^2\), so likelihood maximization equals mean-squared-error minimization. Unknown or heteroscedastic variance requires an extension; squared loss is not the only model for continuous responses.

For a nonnegative integer count \(y\ge 0\), the Poisson model is \(p(y|\lambda )=\lambda ^ye^{-\lambda }/y\)!. Its canonical parameter is \(\theta =\log\lambda\), predictor \(\eta =\theta\), and inverse link \(\lambda =e^\eta\). The exponential maps every real predictor to a positive mean and gives log likelihood Σ[yη-e^η-log(y!)], whose gradient is the covariate times observed minus predicted count.

Poisson conditional independence says that bins or samples are independent after conditioning on all included covariates; it does not say that real spike trains lack refractoriness or coupling. Adding past spikes to the design matrix models history dependence conditionally. Bin size also sets response support: a longer window permits count>1, while a very small bin is closer to Bernoulli.
keyPoints: The linear component of a GLM is the predictor; the inverse link may make the mean nonlinear.
A Gaussian identity link corresponds to squared error, while a Poisson log link enforces a positive count mean.
Likelihood assumptions include response support and conditional independence and must match the binning scheme.

derivation.title: Deriving the Poisson Log Likelihood and Gradient from the Probability Mass
derivation.setup: Use P independent observations \(y_\mu\), predictors \(\eta _\mu =x_\mu ^\mathrm{T}\beta\), and means \(\lambda _\mu =e^{\eta _\mu }\).

steps.title: Write the Joint Likelihood and Take Its Log
steps.explanation: Independent observation probabilities multiply; the logarithm converts their product into a sum.

steps.title: Differentiate with Respect to the Predictor
steps.explanation: The derivative of \(y\eta\) is y, that of \(-e^\eta\) is \(-e^\eta =-\lambda\), and the factorial term is independent of \(\beta\).

steps.title: Apply the Chain Rule to the Coefficients
steps.explanation: Because \(\partial \eta _\mu /\partial \beta =x_\mu\), each sample contributes its covariate times its count residual.

symbolNotes: \(\lambda _\mu\) is the expected count per observation window. If the model output is a rate in spikes/s, multiply by bin width to obtain the count mean.
log(y!) affects the absolute likelihood and model comparison but not the \(\beta\) gradient; it cannot be discarded when reporting the likelihood value.
derivation.unitsCheck: Both \(\eta\) and log\(\lambda\) must be dimensionless. An expected event count is dimensionless; a continuous-time rate enters the Poisson mean only after multiplication by \(\Delta t\).
derivation.limitCheck: If data variance greatly exceeds its mean, the Poisson model may be overdispersed; a negative-binomial or latent-state model may fit better.

workedExample.title: The Direction of a One-Coefficient Poisson Update
workedExample.problem: For one observation \(x=2\) and \(\beta =0\), \(\eta =0\) and \(\lambda =1\); the observed count is \(y=3\). Find this observation's contribution to the log-likelihood gradient with respect to \(\beta\).
steps: \(\eta =x\beta =0\), and the inverse log link gives \(\lambda =e^0=1\).
The count residual \(y-\lambda =2\).
The gradient contribution is \(x(y-\lambda )=2\times 2=4\), which is positive; gradient ascent raises \(\beta\) and therefore the predicted count.
workedExample.result: A Poisson gradient uses observed minus expected count to set direction, scaled by the covariate magnitude that determines this sample's influence on the coefficient.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If \(y=0\), the same sample gives gradient \(2(0-1)=-2\), lowering \(\beta\) and \(\lambda\) while the prediction remains positive.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is the identity link \(\lambda =\eta\) structurally unsuitable for \(a \operatorname{Poisson} GLM\)?
selfCheck.answer: The linear predictor \(\eta\) may be any real number, so an identity link permits negative expected counts. The log link \(\lambda =e^\eta\) maps the whole real line to positive means and yields the convenient residual gradient of the canonical Poisson likelihood.

pitfalls: Treating Gaussian, Poisson, and Bernoulli as merely three loss names without checking response support and variance assumptions.
Inferring from a conditional Poisson model that real spikes have no refractory period or shared network fluctuation.

modules.title: Retinal Population Filters, Bernoulli Logit, and Conditional Dependence
modules.guidingQuestion: How can one predictor include external stimulus, a neuron's own history, and the past spikes of other neurons, while choosing appropriately between count and binary observations?
paragraphs: For each neuron i, a retinal population GLM forms η_i(t)=k_i*s(t)+h_i*y_i(t-past)+Σ_{j≠i}c_{ij}*y_j(t-past)\(+b_{i}\). Stimulus filter \(k_{i}\) describes receptive-field drive. Self-history filter \(h_{i}\) may be negative at short post-spike lags for refractoriness and positive later for burst tendency. Coupling filter \(c_{ij}\) describes how past spikes of other neurons affect the conditional rate of i.

All filters should be fit jointly. Omitting self-history can make the stimulus filter absorb refractory structure; omitting shared stimulus can make a coupling filter mislabel common stimulus drive as interaction. Even with simultaneous fitting, unobserved neurons and global state can leave residual coupling. A coefficient therefore measures predictive conditional dependence, not an anatomical synapse.

In a very small bin, \(y_{t}\in {0,1}\) and a Bernoulli likelihood is suitable. Use log odds \(\theta =\log[q/(1-q)]\) as predictor \(\eta\), with inverse link \(q=e^\eta /(1+e^\eta )\). At \(\eta =0\), \(q=0.5\); increasing \(\eta\) by one multiplies the odds by e. That statement is more accurate than a fixed probability increment because sigmoid slope differs near 0 and near 1.

Bernoulli negative log likelihood is binary cross-entropy. It can model either small-bin spike/no-spike observations or behavioral classification, but their observation units and covariates differ. For continuous-time rate r, the Poisson bin mean is \(\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}=r\Delta t\). When \(\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}\ll 1\), \(q=1-e^{-\lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}}\approx \lambda _{\mathrm{bin}}\approx r\Delta t\). If \(\lambda\) in the previous module already denotes expected count per bin, do not multiply by \(\Delta t\) again. Bernoulli loses count information once multiple spikes per bin are appreciable. Before selecting a model, state whether each observation is a count window, binary bin, or behavioral trial.
keyPoints: A population predictor may include stimulus, self-history, cross-neuron history, and a bias simultaneously.
A coupling filter is a conditional statistical coefficient, not automatically a direct excitatory or inhibitory synapse.
The Bernoulli logit maps to probability; the small-bin Poisson approximation requires a very small expected count.

derivation.title: From Bernoulli Likelihood to the Sigmoid and Cross-Entropy
derivation.setup: For one observation \(y\in {0,1}\) with spike probability q, use logit predictor \(\eta =\log[q/(1-q)]=x^\mathrm{T}\beta\).

steps.title: Solve for the Inverse Link
steps.explanation: Starting with \(q/(1-q)=e^\eta\) and rearranging gives \(q=e^\eta /(1+e^\eta )=1/(1+e^{-\eta })\).

steps.title: Write the Log Likelihood
steps.explanation: Taking the logarithm of Bernoulli probability \(q^y(1-q)^{1-y}\) gives \(y\log q+(1-y)\log(1-q)\).

steps.title: Identify the Residual Gradient
steps.explanation: The sigmoid derivative \(q(1-q)\) cancels the derivatives of the log terms, yielding \(\partial \ell /\partial \eta =y-q\); multiplication by x gives the coefficient gradient.

symbolNotes: q is the probability of at least one spike in the current bin. If y denotes a behavioral choice, it instead means choice probability.
Odds q/(1-q) differ from probability. Holding other covariates fixed, coefficient \(\beta _{j}\) means that increasing \(x_{j}\) by one unit multiplies the odds by \(e^{\beta _{j}}\).
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\eta\) and log odds are dimensionless. A covariate with physical units therefore needs a reciprocal-unit coefficient so \(x_{j}\beta _{j}\) is dimensionless.
derivation.limitCheck: As q approaches 0 or 1, sigmoid slope \(q(1-q)\) becomes small. Complete separation can make unregularized logistic coefficients diverge.

workedExample.title: Combining History Filters into a Conditional Spike Probability
workedExample.problem: A bin's predictor consists of bias -2, stimulus contribution +1.5, refractory self-history -3, and coupling from another neuron +0.5. Compute \(\eta\) and q, then remove the refractory term and compare.
steps: Without the refractory term, \(\eta =0\) and \(q=0.5\).
Thus a strong negative filter from the neuron's recent spike can suppress immediate spike probability even in the presence of stimulus and coupling drive.
workedExample.result: A GLM adds evidence from different sources in predictor space, then uses a sigmoid to convert the total into a valid probability.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Contributions add in log-odds space, not as probabilities. Directly adding probabilities can exceed 1.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does fitting stimulus and coupling filters jointly still not justify interpreting a coupling coefficient as a causal synapse?
selfCheck.answer: The model controls only measured covariates. Unobserved common input, global state, model mismatch, and indirect network paths can still create conditional dependence. Establishing a causal synapse additionally requires intervention, anatomy, or stronger identifiability assumptions.

pitfalls: Including current or future spikes in a history design matrix, causing information leakage and falsely high predictive performance.
Interpreting a log-odds coefficient as a fixed additive change in probability and ignoring the sigmoid operating point.

objectives: Distinguish Barlow's three hypotheses accurately and present efficient coding as a normative proposal constrained by noise and resources.
Explain surprise=\(-\log p\) from the additivity of information for independent events, and compute entropy, conditional entropy, and mutual information.
Derive the joint-distribution form of mutual information, show that \(I=0\) under independence, and explain why differential entropy can be negative and depends on coordinate units.
Starting from \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), derive input and output covariance while distinguishing signal, input noise, and output noise by their locations in the encoder.

Explain the Gaussian-MI determinant formula, fixed-information constraints, channel capacity, decorrelation, and orthogonal nonuniqueness, and show how added symmetries can select center-surround filters.
prerequisiteBridge: A probability \(p(x)\) lies between 0 and 1. A logarithm converts multiplication into addition: log_b(pq)=log_bp+log_bq. An expectation is a probability-weighted average. A discrete random variable X assigns probabilities to outcomes; joint \(p(x,y)\) and conditional \(p(y|x)=p(x,y)/p(x)\) describe relations between two variables.

Covariance \(C=E[(x-E[x])(x-E[x])^\mathrm{T}]\) describes multivariate spread. Under \(y=Ax\), covariance becomes \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive-noise covariances add. For a Gaussian distribution, the determinant measures the scale of the covariance ellipsoid's volume, so the log determinant measures changes in multidimensional uncertainty.

A normative model asks which code is optimal under an explicit objective and explicit constraints. It does not by itself explain how evolution, development, or synaptic mechanisms attain that code. Efficient coding must accommodate input redundancy, input noise, output noise, and finite firing or channel cost. Pursuing output decorrelation alone can amplify noise.

diagnostic.prompt: With logarithms base 2, what is the surprise of an outcome with probability 1/8?
diagnostic.explanation: Three independent fair binary choices are required to reduce the probability to 1/8, so observing the outcome conveys 3 bits. Changing the logarithm base changes the numerical unit.

diagnostic.prompt: Let X be fair Bernoulli and \(Y=X\). What are \(H(X)\), \(H(X|Y)\), and \(I(X;Y)\)?
diagnostic.explanation: Once Y is known, X is known exactly and conditional uncertainty is zero. High entropy in Y does not imply low redundancy between the two variables.

diagnostic.prompt: Let \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\), with every term zero-mean and the noises independent. How should \(C_{y}\) be written?
diagnostic.answer: \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\); for isotropic noise, \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+\sigma _{x}^2I)A^\mathrm{T}+\sigma _{y}^2I\).
diagnostic.explanation: Signal and input noise both pass through A, whereas output noise is added afterward. The two noise sources therefore cannot be placed at the same point in the model.

diagnostic.prompt: After whitening makes covariance I, why does left multiplication by any orthogonal U leave output covariance equal to I?
diagnostic.answer: Because \(U I U^\mathrm{T}=UU^\mathrm{T}=I\).
diagnostic.explanation: Second-order decorrelation requires normalized orthogonal axes but does not uniquely specify their spatial form. Center-surround filters require translation or rotation symmetry, locality, or other constraints.

modules.title: Barlow's Hypotheses and the Foundations of Information Theory
modules.guidingQuestion: How can the idea that a sensory system should not waste spikes on predictable content be converted into quantitative measures of uncertainty and dependence?
paragraphs: The source notes retain three ideas from Barlow: detect “passwords” of critical significance, filter signals for other nervous-system regions, and recode sensory messages to reduce redundancy. This lecture focuses on the third. Efficient coding explains why a code is advantageous under specified input statistics, noise, and cost. It is a normative hypothesis; the same receptive field may also have developmental, biophysical, or task-specific explanations.

Surprise for one outcome should increase as its probability decreases, and surprises for independent events should add. Because their joint probability is pq, the continuous monotone solution of \(S(pq)=S(p)+S(q)\) is \(S(p)=-\log_{bp}\). Base 2 gives bits and base e gives nats; an event of probability 1 has zero surprise.

Entropy \(H(X)=E[-\log p(X)]\) is expected surprise before observation. Conditional entropy \(H(Y|X)\) averages the remaining uncertainty in Y at each x. Mutual information \(I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y|X)\) is the average reduction in uncertainty about Y after observing X, equivalently \(\sum p(x,y)\log(p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y)))\). It detects every statistical dependence, not only linear correlation.

If X and Y are independent, the joint ratio equals 1, \(\log 1=0\), and \(I=0\). Under standard discrete or continuous definitions, the converse also holds almost everywhere. For a continuous variable, differential entropy \(h=-\int f \log f\) uses density \(f(x)\); it can be negative and changes with measurement units. Mutual information is an entropy difference whose coordinate-scaling terms cancel, making it more stable than differential entropy alone.
keyPoints: Efficient coding is constrained optimization, not the unique mechanism behind every sensory feature.
The logarithmic form of surprise follows because independent probabilities multiply while their information adds.
Entropy is average uncertainty; mutual information is the average reduction in one variable's uncertainty provided by another.

derivation.title: Equivalent Forms of Mutual Information and Independence
derivation.setup: Consider discrete X,Y, with all probabilities used on their support positive and \(p(x,y)=p(x)p(y|x)\).

steps.title: Expand the Difference of Entropies
steps.explanation: Write both \(H(Y)\) and \(H(Y|X)\) as sums weighted by the same joint probability \(p(x,y)\).

steps.title: Combine the Logarithms
steps.explanation: Turn the difference of logarithms into a log ratio and substitute \(p(y|x)=p(x,y)/p(x)\).

steps.title: Substitute Independence
steps.explanation: When \(p(x,y)=p(x)p(y)\), every nonzero term has ratio=1 and all contributions vanish.

symbolNotes: By continuity, \(0 \log 0\) is defined as 0. Support mismatches need special care; division by zero is not valid.
The log base determines the unit of MI, so bits and nats cannot be added within one report.
derivation.unitsCheck: Probabilities and their ratios are dimensionless, making the logarithm valid. A differential density has reciprocal units, which is why a standalone differential entropy depends on coordinate units.
derivation.limitCheck: A deterministic continuous relation can yield infinite MI in the ideal zero-noise limit. Finite measurement noise and discretization alter the numerical estimate.

workedExample.title: Binary Entropy and Predictability
workedExample.problem: Compute the entropy of \(\operatorname{Bernoulli} p=0.5\) and \(p=0.9\) using \(\log 2\).
steps: At \(p=0.9\) the outcome is more predictable, so expected surprise is lower. This has nothing to do with the numerical mean of the random variable.
workedExample.result: A uniform binary distribution has maximum uncertainty; biasing it toward one outcome lowers entropy.
workedExample.sanityCheck: As \(p\to 1\), \(H\to 0\). Exchanging p with 1-p leaves entropy unchanged because it merely swaps outcome labels.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does negative differential entropy not mean probability theory has failed?
selfCheck.answer: A continuous density is not the probability of one outcome; it may exceed 1, and its entropy contains the coordinate bin size or units. Rescaling a variable adds a log-scale term. Shared scale contributions cancel in MI, which remains nonnegative and retains its dependence interpretation.

pitfalls: Equating high entropy directly with high useful information while ignoring the receiver, task, noise, and conditional structure.
Replacing independence with correlation=0, even though nonlinear dependent variables can have zero linear correlation and \(MI>0\).

modules.title: The Noisy Retina of Atick and Redlich and Covariance Propagation
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a linear retinal encoder transform natural signals and input noise together while preserving decodable information in the presence of output noise?
paragraphs: Atick and Redlich conceptualize the retina as a noisy channel. Photoreceptor or input noise \(\eta _{x}\) is first added to world signal s, giving \(x=s+\eta _{x}\). Retinal processing A acts on x, and RGC or output noise \(\eta _{y}\) is then added, giving \(y=Ax+\eta _{y}\). A is both a spatial filter and a linear recoding from photoreceptor coordinates to output channels.

Assuming signal and noises are zero-mean and mutually independent, \(C_{x}=C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}}\). A linear transformation yields \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\), after which output noise adds: \(C_{y}=A(C_{s}+C_{\eta _{x}})A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\). Input noise is amplified or attenuated together with the signal, while output noise never passes through A; optimal gain therefore cannot be based on signal covariance alone.

Natural-image signals are highly correlated at nearby positions, so \(C_{s}\) typically has long spatial scales. Isotropic white noise can be written \(\sigma _{x}^2I\) and \(\sigma _{y}^2I\). A high-pass or center-surround A can reduce low-frequency redundancy but may relatively amplify high-frequency input noise. Setting A to zero eliminates output redundancy but also removes all signal information, so an information constraint is essential.

The Gaussian assumption makes covariance sufficient to specify the distribution and yields a closed-form mutual information. Real natural images contain edges, heavy tails, and nonstationarity, so the theory is a second-order approximation. Its value is a precise prediction: the optimal spatial profile should vary with the signal-to-noise ratio and channel cost, rather than being an unconditionally optimal fixed center-surround.
keyPoints: Input noise is added before encoder A and is filtered; output noise is added afterward.
Covariance propagates as \(ACA^\mathrm{T}\), and independent additive noises enter at their respective stages.
Redundancy reduction must be constrained jointly by retained information and output cost.

derivation.title: Deriving Output Covariance Step by Step
derivation.setup: Let s, \(\eta _{x}\), and \(\eta _{y}\) be zero-mean and pairwise independent, with \(x=s+\eta _{x}\) and \(y=A x+\eta _{y}\).

steps.title: Find the Input Covariance
steps.explanation: Expand \(E[(s+\eta _{x})(s+\eta _{x})^\mathrm{T}]\). Independence and zero means make the cross-terms vanish.

steps.title: Pass Through the Linear Encoder
steps.explanation: For \(z=Ax\), \(C_{z}=E[Axx^\mathrm{T}A^\mathrm{T}]=AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\). The formula remains valid for rectangular A.

steps.title: Add Output Noise
steps.explanation: Because \(\eta _{y}\) and Ax are independent, their covariance matrices add directly.

symbolNotes: If input has N dimensions and output has M channels, then \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times N}\), \(C_{x}\) is N×N, and \(C_{y}\) is M×M.
Isotropic noise \(\sigma ^2I\) is an assumption; correlated noise requires its full covariance matrix.
derivation.unitsCheck: If s and x are dimensionless contrast and A has units output/contrast, then \(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\mathrm{output}^2\) units and can be added to \(C_{\eta _{y}}\).
derivation.limitCheck: When \(\eta _{x}\) correlates with s or noise depends on the stimulus, cross-terms do not vanish and the simple independent additive model fails.

workedExample.title: Transforming Signal and Noise Together in a Two-Dimensional Encoder
workedExample.problem: Let \(C_{s}=\operatorname{diag}(9,1)\), input noise \(C_\eta x=I\), \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,2)\), and output noise \(C_\eta y=0.25I\). Find \(C_{y}\).
steps: \(C_{x}=C_{s}+I=\operatorname{diag}(10,2)\).
\(AC_{x}A^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 10,2^2\times 2)=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)\).
\(C_{y}=\operatorname{diag}(2.5,8)+\operatorname{diag}(0.25,0.25)=\operatorname{diag}(2.75,8.25)\).
workedExample.result: A suppresses the first coordinate and amplifies the second, while output noise adds the same 0.25 variance on both axes.
workedExample.sanityCheck: For \(A=0\), only 0.25I remains in \(C_{y}\). The output appears decorrelated but contains no s, showing that decorrelation alone is not a valid objective.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does moving input and output noise into one term before A change the optimization?
selfCheck.answer: A reshapes input noise, so increasing gain at one frequency also amplifies its input noise. Output noise does not pass through A, and increasing gain can improve signal relative to output noise. Their effects on the gain tradeoff differ and cannot be merged.

pitfalls: Omitting \(A^\mathrm{T}\) in covariance propagation, producing a nonsymmetric result or incorrect output shape.
Treating a Gaussian second-order model as the full natural-image distribution and ignoring edges and higher-order dependencies.

modules.title: Gaussian Information, Nonunique Decorrelation, and the Selection of Center-Surround Filters
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does retaining fixed information while reducing output redundancy favor whitening yet fail to determine a unique receptive-field shape?
paragraphs: For a d-dimensional Gaussian z, \(h(z)=1/2 \log[(2\pi e)^d \det C_{z}]\). In \(y=As+A\eta _{x}+\eta _{y}\), conditioning on s turns As into a known shift, leaving \(C_{y|s}=AC_{\eta _{x}}A^\mathrm{T}+C_{\eta _{y}}\); unconditional \(C_{y}\) also includes \(AC_{s}A^\mathrm{T}\). Substitution into \(I(y;s)=h(y)-h(y|s)\) cancels the two factors \((2\pi e)^d\) and gives \(I(y;s)=1/2 \log[\det C_{y}/\det C_{y|s}]\). The determinant is the product of covariance eigenvalues, so this ratio compares total output uncertainty volume with noise-only volume rather than any single variance.

Atick and Redlich first require retained information \(I(y;s)=I^{*}\le I(x;s)\), then reduce redundancy under fixed output power or dynamic range. Let \(w=Ax\) denote the encoder signal before output noise and \(y=w+\eta _{y}\). The source notes therefore write output-channel capacity as \(C_{\mathrm{out}}=\max_{p(w)}\) \(I(y;w)\). The objective \(R=1-I(y;s)/C_{\mathrm{out}}\) penalizes spending channel capacity to retransmit the same information. A basis with diagonal output covariance has no second-order correlations; with fixed total power and isotropic output noise, distributing variance more evenly can increase Gaussian channel capacity. The aim is not unconstrained entropy maximization but code optimization under information, noise, and output-range constraints.

A whitening transform V satisfies \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=I\). For any orthogonal U, \((UV)C_{x}(UV)^\mathrm{T}=UIU^\mathrm{T}=I\), so the pre-output-noise whitened code may be rotated without changing covariance. Full Gaussian MI is also unchanged only if output noise is isotropic, \(C_{\eta _{y}}=\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), or absent; then total and conditional-noise covariances undergo the same orthogonal similarity transformation. With anisotropic output noise, rotating the encoder changes signal alignment with the noise axes and generally changes MI. Decorrelation alone therefore identifies a family of solutions, not a unique localized center-surround shape for each neuron.

Additional translation invariance, rotational symmetry, local wiring, or identical-channel constraints can select an isotropic center-surround member of that family. This prediction makes center-surround filtering compatible with natural statistics but is not unique causal proof. The real retina must also handle optics, photoreceptor low-pass filtering, adaptation, and non-Gaussian scenes; the next lecture's SNR-dependent filter follows from these constraints.
keyPoints: The determinant ratio in Gaussian MI compares total output covariance with conditional noise covariance.
Whitening and decorrelation are nonunique under orthogonal rotations.
A unique center-surround form requires symmetry, locality, or other additional constraints; redundancy reduction alone does not imply it.

derivation.title: From Gaussian Entropy to an Information Constraint and Rotation Ambiguity
derivation.setup: Let d-dimensional output y and signal s be jointly Gaussian, with conditional covariance \(C_{y|s}\) independent of the particular s. Then let V satisfy \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=I\) and U be orthogonal. Rotation invariance of whitened covariance requires no extra condition; rotation invariance of full Gaussian MI additionally requires \(C_{\eta _{y}}=\sigma _{y}^{2}I\) or no output noise.

steps.title: Write Gaussian Differential Entropy
steps.explanation: Gaussian uncertainty is determined by the covariance ellipsoid. Dimension d supplies a common constant, while the determinant combines variances along every principal axis.

steps.title: Subtract to Obtain Mutual Information
steps.explanation: \(I(y;s)=h(y)-h(y|s)\). Because the dimensions match, \((2\pi e)^d\) cancels and only the determinant ratio of total output covariance to conditional noise covariance remains.
steps.latex: I(\mathbf y;\mathbf s)=\frac12\log\!\frac{\det C_y}{\det C_{y\mid s}}

steps.title: State the Retained-Information and Output Constraints
steps.explanation: The normative problem does not maximize entropy without qualification. It first requires retained information \(I^{*}\), then constrains output power or dynamic range and compares redundancy under those constraints.
steps.latex: I(\mathbf y;\mathbf s)=I^*,\qquad \operatorname{tr}C_y\le P_{\max},\qquad R=1-\frac{I(\mathbf y;\mathbf s)}{C_{\mathrm{out}}}

steps.title: Construct Another Encoder
steps.explanation: Set \(A'=UV\): V whitens first, then U rotates the axes of the whitened output space.

steps.title: Propagate the Covariance
steps.explanation: Substitute A' into \(A'C_{x}A'^\mathrm{T}\) and group factors using associativity of matrix multiplication.

steps.title: Use Orthogonality
steps.explanation: The middle covariance is I, giving \(UIU^\mathrm{T}=UU^\mathrm{T}=I\). Every U satisfies the same second-order objective.

steps.title: State the Noise Condition Needed for MI Invariance
steps.explanation: With isotropic output noise, total and conditional-noise covariance before and after rotation are related by orthogonal similarity transformations, preserving their determinant ratio. Anisotropic output noise does not permit this step.
steps.latex: C_{\eta_y}=\sigma_y^2 I\;\Longrightarrow\; C'_{y\mid s}=U(C_{w\mid s}+\sigma_y^2I)U^{\mathsf T}

symbolNotes: d is output dimension. \(C_{y}\) contains signal and noise; \(C_{y|s}\) is the noise covariance remaining after signal is specified.
\(I^{*}\) is the task-required information, while \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\) is channel capacity under output noise and a power constraint; they are not the same quantity.
An orthogonal rotation preserves Euclidean length and identity covariance but does not imply that biological receptive fields can perform arbitrary global mixing at no cost.
A covariance determinant is the product of its eigenvalues. A zero eigenvalue collapses the Gaussian volume.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\det C_{y}\) and \(\det C_{y|s}\) share units output-units^{2d}, so their ratio and its logarithm are dimensionless. Whitening usually standardizes outputs to unit variance; retaining physical units requires an additional scale matrix.
derivation.limitCheck: For singular covariance, restrict the log determinant to the supported subspace or regularize it. Non-Gaussian components can remain dependent even when covariance is I, allowing higher-order objectives to break the rotational degeneracy.

workedExample.title: Rotation Ambiguity in Two-Dimensional Whitening
workedExample.problem: Let \(C_{x}=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)\), \(V=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1)\), and 45° rotation \(U=(1/\sqrt 2)[[1,-1],[1,1]]\). Compare the pre-output-noise code covariances of V and UV, then state when MI is also invariant.
steps: \(VC_{x}V^\mathrm{T}=\operatorname{diag}((1/2)^2\times 4,1)=I\).
With \(A'=UV\), \(A'C_{x}A'^\mathrm{T}=U I U^\mathrm{T}=I\).

The outputs of V align with the original axes, whereas those of UV are 45° mixtures of the two whitened coordinates. Before output noise, both have decorrelated unit variance. If subsequent noise is \(\sigma _{y}^{2}I\), adding it also contributes the same \(\sigma _{y}^{2}\) on both output axes.
workedExample.result: One covariance objective permits different filter axes. Preferring localized center-surround filters requires additional spatial constraints.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If U is not orthogonal—for example, if its first row is multiplied by 2—the pre-noise covariance is no longer I. If output-noise covariance is anisotropic, orthogonal U alone also does not imply invariant MI.

selfCheck.prompt: What crucial conditions are missing from the statement “decorrelation produces center-surround filters”?
selfCheck.answer: Decorrelation requires only a diagonal or whitened output covariance, and any subsequent orthogonal rotation satisfies it equally well. Translation and rotation symmetry, locality, wiring, noise, or cost constraints are needed to select center-surround filters from the equivalent solutions.

pitfalls: Claiming that more output entropy or channel capacity is unconditionally better while ignoring fixed information, noise, and firing cost.
Treating the normative prediction of center-surround filtering as unique evidence for its anatomical or developmental mechanism.

objectives: Explain from the relative strengths of input signal and noise why decorrelating filters are appropriate at high SNR while spatial averaging serves a different objective at low SNR.
Express translation-invariant image statistics as a correlation function of displacement alone and explain why complex exponentials are the natural basis of convolution operators.
Derive the convolution theorem and output power-spectrum equation step by step, then infer the frequency trend of a whitening filter from the approximate natural-image spectrum \(1/|\xi |^{2}\).
Design an LNP comparison across illumination levels or stimulus statistics that separates a change in the linear filter, a change in the static nonlinearity, and a mere response-scale change.
prerequisiteBridge: Treat SNR as the ratio between predictable signal variation and unpredictable noise variation, not simply how clear an image looks. If four adjacent receptors receive nearly the same slowly varying signal and each carries independent zero-mean noise, averaging them preserves the common signal but halves the noise standard deviation. Conversely, if genuine high-spatial-frequency structure is strong, excessive averaging erases that structure too. Whether a filter should smooth therefore depends jointly on the input structure and the noise.

A Fourier representation introduces no new physical stimulus; it rewrites the same image as a sum of waves with different frequencies, directions, and phases. Euler's identity \(e^{i\theta }=\cos\theta +i \sin\theta\) combines sine and cosine into one complex exponential. Imaginary numbers are computational bookkeeping, and a real image remains real after reconstruction. The two-dimensional frequency vector \(\xi\) points along the fastest luminance change, while the stripes are perpendicular to \(\xi\). Larger \(|\xi |\) means more oscillations per unit distance. This directional relation is essential for reading power spectra and receptive-field frequency responses.

Recall the three LNP stages: a stimulus is projected through a spatiotemporal filter to produce linear drive; a static nonlinearity turns drive into instantaneous firing rate; and a stochastic spiking process produces spikes. Comparing only mean firing rate across two adaptation conditions cannot distinguish a filter change, nonlinear gain change, or baseline shift. Estimate the linear kernel and input-output curve independently with controlled stimuli in each condition and evaluate predictions on held-out data so that adaptation becomes a falsifiable statement about parameter changes.

diagnostic.prompt: Four adjacent receptors all receive common signal value 8, and each has independent noise with standard deviation 2. After averaging the four, what are the signal mean and noise standard deviation?
diagnostic.answer: The common signal remains 8; the average noise variance is \(4/4=1\), so its standard deviation is 1.
diagnostic.explanation: Averaging does not attenuate a signal identical across the four channels. Independent-noise variances add and are then divided by \(4^{2}\). This is the quantitative reason spatial pooling can improve readability at low SNR.

diagnostic.prompt: A two-dimensional grating is \(\cos(\xi \cdot x)\). Are its equal-luminance stripes parallel or perpendicular to frequency vector \(\xi\)?
diagnostic.answer: Equal-luminance lines have constant \(\xi \cdot x\), so motion along a stripe must leave the dot product unchanged. The stripe direction is perpendicular to \(\xi\).
diagnostic.explanation: \(\xi\) points along fastest phase increase, not along the stripes themselves. Confusing those directions rotates an orientation-tuning interpretation by ninety degrees.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(y(x)=(K*s)(x)\), how is \(\hat{y}(\xi )\) written in the Fourier domain?
diagnostic.answer: \(\hat{y}(\xi )=\hat{K}(\xi )\hat{s}(\xi )\): spatial convolution becomes complex multiplication at each frequency.
diagnostic.explanation: The multiplication magnitude determines amplification or attenuation at that frequency, and its phase determines spatial shift. Each frequency mode can therefore be analyzed independently.

diagnostic.prompt: Suppose the natural-image input spectrum is \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\). If complete whitening is the sole objective, how should \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) vary with \(|\xi |\)?
diagnostic.answer: \(|\hat{K}(\xi )|\) should increase approximately linearly with \(|\xi |\), because \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) must be constant across frequencies.
diagnostic.explanation: That is the ideal noise-free result. Real retinas are also limited by optical low-pass filtering, receptor noise, and metabolic cost, so gain cannot grow without bound at the highest frequencies.

modules.title: SNR Selects the Filtering Objective: Remove Redundancy or Reduce Noise
modules.guidingQuestion: Why might one visual system strengthen center-surround filtering in bright conditions but behave more like a spatial averager in dim conditions?
paragraphs: Page 1 interprets filter shape along an SNR axis. At high SNR, input detail is reliable relative to internal and photon noise. Neighboring pixels are then strongly correlated, and transmitting them unchanged wastes limited output dynamic range on repeated information. An excitatory-center, inhibitory-surround difference kernel suppresses common slow components while retaining edges, reducing output correlations. A strong surround is a normative prediction under specified statistics and costs; it does not alone establish its synaptic implementation.

At low SNR, differencing creates another problem: subtracting two channels removes their common signal but imports both independent noise sources into the result. When genuine high-frequency signal is already buried in noise, amplifying high frequencies wastes firing range. Spatial pooling sums or averages nearby measurements. Shared low-frequency structure adds coherently, whereas independent noise adds in variance, raising output SNR. A broad same-sign receptive field is then more useful than a sharp center-surround.

Intermediate SNR creates a continuous tradeoff, not a hard switch. Distinguish amplitude \(SNR_{\mathrm{amp}}=S/\sigma\) from power \(SNR_{\mathrm{power}}=P_{s}/P_{n}\); for the same linear measurement and bandwidth, \(SNR_{\mathrm{power}}=SNR_{\mathrm{amp}}^{2}\). The pooling derivation below uses amplitude SNR, so averaging n independent noisy measurements improves it by \(\sqrt n\). Spectral analysis uses \(P_{s}(\xi )/P_{n}(\xi )\). Where this ratio is high, the filter can spend gain correcting redundancy; where it is low, gain should shrink. SNR differs across spatial frequencies, so dimmer light can broaden pooling, weaken the surround, and change total gain rather than merely scaling the whole filter.

Read the page's graph as a conditional prediction. First establish that the axis or curves denote SNR rather than time; then compare center and surround areas and widths; finally state measurable outcomes, such as reduced high-frequency gain and a broader estimated receptive field in low light. A fall in firing rate alone does not show that the filter broadened, since a higher nonlinear threshold or fewer available spikes can produce the same observation.
keyPoints: At high SNR, reliable high-frequency information lets center-surround differencing reduce redundancy across neighboring channels.
At low SNR, spatial averaging preserves common signal and lowers independent-noise standard deviation at the cost of spatial resolution.
Adaptation should be described as frequency-dependent changes in filter and nonlinearity, not only as a change in mean firing rate.

derivation.title: How Noise Shrinks When n Neighboring Measurements Are Averaged
derivation.setup: Let each channel be \(x_{j}=s+\epsilon _{j}\), with locally common signal s and independent noise \(\epsilon _{j}\) of \(\operatorname{mean} 0\) and variance \(\sigma ^{2}\). Define \(y=(1/n)\sum _j x_{j}\).

steps.title: Separate Common Signal from Noise
steps.explanation: Substitute every \(x_{j}\) into the average. The common signal appears n times and remains s after division by n; the remaining term is the mean of n noise values.

steps.title: Compute the Variance of the Averaged Noise
steps.explanation: Independence eliminates cross-covariances, so the variance of the sum is the sum of variances. The factor 1/n becomes \(1/n^{2}\) in the variance.

steps.title: Convert to Standard Deviation and SNR
steps.explanation: Taking the square root gives standard deviation \(\sigma /\sqrt n\). If signal amplitude is unchanged, amplitude divided by noise standard deviation—and hence amplitude SNR—increases by \(\sqrt n\).

symbolNotes: Independent noise is an assumption. Positive noise correlations make the variance reduction smaller than 1/n.
The locally common-signal assumption applies only to components varying more slowly than the pooling radius; averaging attenuates fine edges.
derivation.unitsCheck: x, s, \(\epsilon\), and y share luminance or voltage units. n and SNR are dimensionless; variance has squared signal units.
derivation.limitCheck: For \(n=1\), noise is unchanged. As n grows, independent noise falls, but signal bias increases if the signal varies within the window, so an infinitely large window cannot produce infinite performance.

workedExample.title: Comparing Four-Point Averaging with Neighbor Differencing
workedExample.problem: A flat region has common signal 10 and independent pixel noise of standard deviation 2. Compute the noise standard deviation after averaging four pixels, then for the difference x1-x2.
steps: The four-point average preserves common value 10. Its noise variance is \(2^{2}/4=1\), so standard deviation is 1.
Neighbor differencing cancels the common value, \(10-10=0\). Its noise is \(\epsilon _{1}-\epsilon _{2}\), with variance \(2^{2}+2^{2}=8\).
The difference-noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt 8\approx 2.83\), larger than that of one pixel. This cost is worthwhile only when the edge signal is strong enough.
workedExample.result: Averaging is favored in a low-SNR flat region; strong differencing is justified when SNR is high and reliable edges exist.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If both channels contain identical rather than independent noise, differencing cancels it. The result shows why noise correlation structure must be stated.

selfCheck.prompt: Why should a weaker surround in low light not be summarized as the visual system “no longer caring about edges”?
selfCheck.answer: Edges can remain behaviorally important. The change means that current high-frequency evidence is unreliable relative to noise and strong differencing would amplify noise. The system temporarily sacrifices resolution for a more stable estimate; the behavioral target need not have changed.

pitfalls: Equating high SNR with high mean luminance, even though SNR also depends on frequency, internal noise, and stimulus contrast.
Comparing only receptive-field peaks and ignoring integrated center-surround strength, width, and estimation uncertainty.

modules.title: From Translation-Invariant Statistics to Fourier Diagonalization
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does rewriting an image by spatial frequency allow convolutional filtering to be computed frequency by frequency?
paragraphs: Page 2 describes translation statistics of natural scenes. Across many images, or a sufficiently large stationary image, correlation between two positions depends mainly on displacement \(\Delta x\) rather than absolute coordinates: \(C(x,x')=C(x-x')\). This does not mean every photograph is uniform everywhere; it means the statistical ensemble follows the same rule after translation. Such covariance matrices repeat by displacement. Complex exponential modes retain their frequency under convolution or correlation and change only in complex amplitude, making them a natural basis.

A two-dimensional component \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) carries frequency direction and phase. The dot product \(\xi \cdot x\) projects position onto the frequency vector. Phase changes fastest along \(\xi\) and remains constant in the perpendicular direction, so visible stripes are perpendicular to \(\xi\). A real image uses paired \(+\xi\) and \(-\xi\) components whose imaginary parts cancel. Near the spectrum center are slow variations; farther away are finer spatial structures.

The convolution theorem on page 3 converts \(y(x)=\int K(x-x')s(x')dx'\) into \(\hat{y}(\xi )=\hat{K}(\xi )\hat{s}(\xi )\). Rather than memorizing it, expand the Fourier integral, exchange integration order, and set \(u=x-x'\). The \(\operatorname{exponential} e^{-i\xi \cdot (u+x')}\) then factors into one term in u and one in x', leaving the two integrals \(\hat{K}\) and ŝ. Every \(\xi\) multiplies independently, diagonalizing the large translation-invariant linear operator.

\(\hat{K}(\xi )\) is generally complex. Its magnitude \(|\hat{K}|\) is the gain at that frequency and its argument is the phase shift. A symmetric center-surround kernel often has phase near zero or \(\pi\), making its amplitude response prominent. Asymmetric receptive fields and temporal delays carry important phase information. A spatial thumbnail alone makes it difficult to tell whether a receptive field favors slow gradients, edges, or a particular band.
keyPoints: Translation-invariant covariance depends only on positional difference, making Fourier modes statistically nonmixing directions.
Frequency vector \(\xi\) is perpendicular to image stripes, and \(|\xi |\) sets spatial oscillation speed.
Convolution becomes frequencywise complex multiplication; magnitude controls gain and phase angle controls shift.

derivation.title: Deriving the Convolution Theorem Term by Term
derivation.setup: Define \(y(x)=\int K(x-x')s(x')dx'\) and adopt Fourier convention \(\hat{f}(\xi )=\int f(x)e^{-i\xi \cdot x}dx\).

steps.title: Insert the Convolution into the Output Fourier Transform
steps.explanation: Substitute the integral for y into ŷ and write the integrations over x and x' in one expression.

steps.title: Change Variables to Relative Displacement
steps.explanation: Set \(u=x-x'\), so \(x=u+x'\) and \(dx=du\). The exponential factors into a term depending on u and one depending on x'.

steps.title: Identify the Two Fourier Transforms
steps.explanation: The u integral is \(\hat{K}(\xi )\), and the x' integral is \(\hat{s}(\xi )\); their product is the output frequency component.
steps.latex: \hat y(\xi)=\left[\int K(u)e^{-i\xi\cdot u}du\right]\left[\int s(x')e^{-i\xi\cdot x'}dx'\right]=\hat K(\xi)\hat s(\xi)

symbolNotes: \(\xi\) has units radians per degree or radians per distance. With cycles per degree, the Fourier exponential includes \(2\pi\).
Writing \(K(x-x')\) means that the weight from input position x' to output position x depends only on relative displacement—the translation-invariance assumption.
derivation.unitsCheck: If spatial integral dx' has area units and y and s share units, K must have inverse-area units. Fourier-transform scale units depend on convention but remain consistent on both sides.
derivation.limitCheck: For a delta-function K, \(\hat{K}=1\) and every frequency passes unchanged. For a broad averaging K, \(\hat{K}\) is concentrated at low frequency, matching the smoothing intuition.

workedExample.title: Passing a Sinusoid Through a Filter with Amplitude and Phase
workedExample.problem: The input is \(s(x)=3\cos(2x)\). At \(\xi =2\) the filter response is \(\hat{K}(2)=0.5e^{-i\pi /4}\). Find the output sinusoid's amplitude and phase shift.
steps: The input contains only the conjugate frequency pair \(\xi =+2\) and \(\xi =-2\), with real-space amplitude 3.
Multiplying each component by \(\hat{K}\) scales amplitude from 3 to 1.5 because its magnitude is 0.5.
The angle \(-\pi /4\) adds phase \(-\pi /4\) to the positive-frequency component, so \(y(x)=1.5\cos(2x-\pi /4)\).
workedExample.result: The filtered sinusoid still has frequency 2, amplitude 1.5, and phase shifted negatively by \(\pi /4\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: A linear translation-invariant filter cannot turn one sinusoid into a new frequency. Obtaining \(\xi =4\) means multiplication was mistaken for a nonlinear square.

selfCheck.prompt: Why do Fourier modes “diagonalize” a translation-invariant linear filter?
selfCheck.answer: After convolution, each input mode \(e^{i\xi \cdot x}\) remains the same \(\xi\) and is multiplied only by complex number \(\hat{K}(\xi )\); distinct \(\xi\) never mix. In this basis, the operator is represented by diagonal gains, one per mode.

pitfalls: Drawing the frequency-vector direction along the stripe direction and thereby rotating the orientation interpretation by ninety degrees.
Using only \(|\hat{K}|\) and discarding phase, even though phase of asymmetric spatial and spatiotemporal kernels controls localization and delay.

modules.title: Natural-Image Power Spectra, Whitening, and Testable Adaptation
modules.guidingQuestion: How does the input statistic \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) predict a filter's frequency profile, and how can an LNP experiment test whether the system actually changes with the environment?
paragraphs: Page 4 approximates the ensemble power spectrum of natural images as \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\): slow luminance variations at low frequencies usually have greater variance than fine high-frequency detail. Linear filtering gives output coefficient \(\hat{K}\hat{s}\) and power \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\). In an ideal model without noise or gain limits, equal output variance across frequencies requires \(|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) to be constant, hence \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). In space, this is a difference structure that suppresses low frequency and relatively enhances edges.

Ideal whitening cannot continue to arbitrarily high frequency. Ocular optics and photoreceptor integration attenuate extreme frequencies, reducing usable signal power. If output noise is approximately flat across frequencies, gain \(|\xi |\) would strongly amplify noise at the highest frequencies. An effective filter therefore often rises over a reliable midfrequency band and falls again when noise dominates, becoming band-pass. As illumination falls, the reliable band contracts and the optimum shifts from stronger center-surround filtering toward smoother pooling.

Page 5 turns this prediction into an LNP measurement. Present sufficiently rich stimuli under high and low light or different spatial correlations, estimate filter \(k_{c}\) separately, and then estimate each condition's nonlinearity \(f_{c}\). Fix a normalization before comparing filters—for example \(||k_{c}||=1\) with signs aligned by the dominant lobe—because multiplying k by a constant and inversely scaling the input axis of f gives identical predictions. Then compare spatial profile, Fourier gain, integrated center-surround ratio, and cross-condition prediction.

Strong evidence comes from distinguishable counterfactuals. If only the nonlinearity changes, the filter from condition A paired with condition B's nonlinearity should approximate data in B. If the filter truly changes, this swap systematically misses particular stimulus directions. Match spike counts or use bootstrap confidence intervals to handle noisier low-light estimates. An adaptation claim should report parameter changes and predictive improvement, not treat two visually different kernel plots as sufficient proof.
keyPoints: Linear filtering yields \(P_{\mathrm{out}}(\xi )=|\hat{K}(\xi )|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\).
For \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\), noise-free whitening gives \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\), but optics and noise force real filters to roll off at high frequency.
Cross-condition LNP comparisons must fix filter scale, estimate each nonlinearity separately, and test parameter swaps on held-out data.

derivation.title: Inferring Whitening Gain from the Input Power Spectrum
derivation.setup: For each \(\xi\), let output coefficient \(\hat{y}=\hat{K}\hat{s}\) and define power as expected squared complex magnitude \(P(\xi )=E[|\hat{s}(\xi )|^{2}]\).

steps.title: Compute Output Power
steps.explanation: A deterministic filter gain leaves the expectation, and the squared magnitude of a complex product is the product of squared magnitudes.

steps.title: Write the Whitening Condition
steps.explanation: Set output variance at every frequency to the same constant c and solve for the required squared gain.

steps.title: Substitute the Natural-Image Approximation
steps.explanation: If \(P_{\mathrm{in}}=a/|\xi |^{2}\), squared gain is \(c|\xi |^{2}/a\); taking the nonnegative square root yields magnitude increasing linearly with \(|\xi |\).

symbolNotes: \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) is an ensemble-average power, not a fixed value for every frequency in one image.
Whitening determines \(|\hat{K}|\) but not phase. Spatial locality, causality, and other constraints further restrict realizable K.
derivation.unitsCheck: If input and output share signal units, \(|\hat{K}|\) is dimensionless gain. P has \(\mathrm{signal}^{2}\) units, and c has the same units as \(P_{\mathrm{out}}\).
derivation.limitCheck: As \(|\xi |\to 0\), ideal gain tends to zero, removing the global mean. As \(|\xi |\to \infty\), the formula diverges, exposing its noise-free infinite-bandwidth assumptions; a real system must regularize.

workedExample.title: Whitening Two Frequencies and Its Noise Cost
workedExample.problem: Let \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(1)=16\) and \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(4)=1\), and require output signal power 4 at both frequencies. Find both gains. Then assume post-input noise power 1 at each frequency and compute output noise powers.
steps: From \(|K|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}=4\), the low-frequency gain is \(|K(1)|=\sqrt{4/16}=0.5\).
The high-frequency gain is \(|K(4)|=\sqrt{4/1}=2\), consistent with a fourfold frequency difference and a fourfold gain difference.
Noise is also multiplied by squared gain, so low-frequency output noise is 0.25 and high-frequency output noise is 4. Although signal powers are equalized, high-frequency SNR remains worse.
workedExample.result: Pure whitening uses gains 0.5 and 2, but the latter amplifies equal input noise to 16 times the former's power, so a noise-aware solution must suppress high frequency.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Substitution confirms equal signal powers: \(0.5^{2}\times 16=4\) and \(2^{2}\times 1=4\).

selfCheck.prompt: Why must an LNP filter's scale convention be fixed before comparing two adaptation conditions?
selfCheck.answer: Multiplying k by constant a while dividing the nonlinearity's horizontal axis by a gives identical firing predictions. Without fixing ||k|| or another convention, an apparent gain change can be only parameterization nonuniqueness.

pitfalls: Treating \(1/|\xi |^{2}\) as an exact law for every natural image rather than an approximate trend over an ensemble.
Directly comparing noisy filter images in a low-spike condition without resampling uncertainty or held-out prediction to rule out estimation variance.

objectives: Distinguish linear selectivity in simple cells from phase invariance in complex cells, and explain why an even-symmetric response can drive the first-order STA toward zero.
Derive phase invariance step by step from the two linear outputs of a quadrature pair while stating the amplitude and orientation dependence that remains.
Separate task training of an optimized model from evaluation of neural predictivity, and design a comparison that never leaks test neural data.
Write the fixed-point equations and nullclines of an E/I rate network and analyze how surround input can produce suppression without raising inhibitory rate.
Use local stability to define an inhibition-stabilized network and avoid reducing ISN to “strong inhibition.”
prerequisiteBridge: Imagine a Gabor-like filter as a template of alternating positive and negative bands. The inner product is positive when bright bars align with positive weights and dark bars with negative weights. Translating the grating by half a period reverses the sign. A simple cell may retain this phase sign, while a complex cell often fires at several phases of the same orientation. If the response is identical for s and -s, positive and negative examples occur in pairs among spike-triggered stimuli and cancel in an ordinary average. The neuron remains selective; the first-order statistic uses the wrong coordinates.

Comparing a model with neural data involves two distinct fits. First, network weights may be trained on a task such as object classification, defining representation \(z(x)\). Second, part of the neural dataset fits a simple mapping from z to neuronal responses, which is evaluated on stimuli excluded from that fit. Classification accuracy asks whether the network performs the task. Neural predictivity asks whether an internal representation relates to recorded responses through a linear or otherwise specified mapping. The scores may correlate, but neither logically guarantees the other.

E/I dynamics require only first-order differential equations and intersections of two lines. Treat \(r_{E}\) and \(r_{I}\) as time-varying population firing rates. Points satisfying \(dr/dt=0\) form a nullcline; the two nullclines intersect at a fixed point. Arrow direction follows the signs of the derivatives. Stability means that the vector field pushes small perturbations back, not that one drawn curve looks steep. Eigenvalues of the linearization provide the local criterion.

diagnostic.prompt: A neuron responds identically to filter projections z and -z. Why can the first-order average of spike-triggered stimuli be nearly zero?
diagnostic.answer: Spikes select large projections on both the positive and negative sides. With a symmetric stimulus distribution, the two trigger means point in opposite directions and cancel.
diagnostic.explanation: A zero STA rules out one signed linear direction as a complete account, not selectivity for |z| or \(z^{2}\). STC or an energy feature can detect the latter.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), does \(L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}\) depend on phase \(\phi\)?
diagnostic.answer: No. Since \(\cos^{2}\phi +\sin^{2}\phi =1\), the sum of squares is always \(A^{2}\).
diagnostic.explanation: A quadrature pair turns phase into rotation of a two-dimensional vector; the squared sum reads its length and ignores its direction.

diagnostic.prompt: Must a network with higher classification accuracy predict visual-cortical responses better?
diagnostic.answer: No. Task performance constrains only the final behavioral output, while internal representations may differ. Predictivity must be tested separately on held-out neural stimuli.
diagnostic.explanation: Choosing a layer, mapping, or network after inspecting test neural data inflates predictivity through selection bias. The evaluation pipeline must keep these data isolated.

diagnostic.prompt: After surround stimulation, both excitatory and inhibitory rates fall. Can recurrent inhibition still contribute to the suppression?
diagnostic.answer: Yes. Surround input can first reduce network excitation, causing the inhibitory population to receive less drive. If E falls more, the net outcome remains suppression.
diagnostic.explanation: A lower I rate does not make inhibition irrelevant. Analyze the recurrent equations, the changed inputs, and the fixed-point shift rather than treating inhibitory firing itself as inhibitory current.

modules.title: From Simple-Cell Pooling to Complex-Cell Energy
modules.guidingQuestion: How can two filters separated by one-quarter period retain orientation selectivity while discarding grating phase?
paragraphs: Page 1 links cascade models to the Hubel–Wiesel construction. If multiple LGN-like center-surround units are arranged along an oblique axis and pooled with same-sign weights, only a light-dark edge matching that arrangement drives many inputs together, producing an elongated simple-cell receptive field. This construction explains the spatial geometry of orientation selectivity but remains sensitive to light-dark position: translating the same grating by half a period reverses the linear projection.

The challenge for a complex cell is phase invariance. If it responds strongly to both positive and negative phases of a grating at one orientation, a linear STA averages the two spike-triggered groups toward zero. Page 2 instead uses two filters separated by 90° of spatial phase—a quadrature pair. As input phase changes, their linear outputs carry energy in turn like two coordinates. Squaring and adding reads vector radius rather than angle.

For a grating matching orientation and spatial frequency, let the two filter projections be \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\), where A depends on contrast and match quality and \(\phi\) is stimulus phase. Energy \(E=L_{1}^{2}+L_{2}^{2}=A^{2}\) is independent of \(\phi\).
