The invariance is conditional: changing orientation or frequency lowers the common projection amplitude A, and changing contrast changes A and hence E. The energy model removes phase, not all stimulus information.

STC can identify these two feature axes as abnormal directions of spike-triggered covariance because spikes select a large radius in the two-dimensional subspace rather than one signed mean direction. The model is still a descriptive cascade of two linear filters, squaring nonlinearities, summation, and perhaps an output nonlinearity. Reproducing several complex-cell responses does not prove that biological synapses implement four anatomically separate stages.
keyPoints: Spatially aligned simple-cell pooling produces orientation selectivity while preserving phase sensitivity.
A complex-cell energy model uses the squared sum of a quadrature pair to turn stimulus phase into an ignored two-dimensional angle.
A zero STA can coexist with strong selectivity; examine covariance or a multifilter subspace in that case.

derivation.title: Why Quadrature Energy Is Invariant to Phase
derivation.setup: For a grating of fixed orientation and frequency, let two normalized filters separated by 90° of phase produce \(L_{1}=A\cos\phi\) and \(L_{2}=A\sin\phi\).

steps.title: Write the Sum of Squares
steps.explanation: The energy stage squares each signed projection separately and adds the two nonnegative results.

steps.title: Factor Out the Common Amplitude
steps.explanation: A does not depend on the current phase, so it can be factored outside the parentheses, leaving the unit-circle identity.

steps.title: Apply the Unit-Circle Identity
steps.explanation: cos\(\phi\) and sin\(\phi\) are the two coordinates of a unit vector. Their squared sum is 1, leaving energy \(A^{2}\).

symbolNotes: A still changes with contrast, orientation mismatch, frequency mismatch, and receptive-field overlap.
Exact invariance assumes truly quadrature filters with matched gains; biological measurements generally approximate this condition.
derivation.unitsCheck: If linear outputs use drive units of spikes/s, their squared sum has \(drive^{2}\) units. A final output nonlinearity can map it back to firing rate.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(A=0\), every phase gives \(E=0\). If the second filter has twice the gain of the first, the squared sum varies with \(\phi\) and phase invariance fails.

workedExample.title: Equal Energy at Three Phases
workedExample.problem: Let \(A=4\) and compute L1, L2, and E at \(\phi =0\), \(\pi /4\), and \(\pi /2\).
steps: For \(\phi =\pi /4\), \(L_{1}=L_{2}=4/\sqrt 2\); each square is 8, hence \(E=16\).
workedExample.result: The linear outputs differ at all three phases, but energy equals 16 each time.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Every pair (L1,L2) lies on a circle of radius 4, and the sum of squares is the squared radius.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does the energy model retain orientation tuning after gaining phase invariance?
selfCheck.answer: Phase rotates the matched quadrature outputs in their two-dimensional plane. Changing orientation reduces both filter projections' common amplitude A, so \(A^{2}\) still falls with orientation mismatch.

pitfalls: Concluding from a near-zero complex-cell STA that the stimulus does not drive the cell, while ignoring positive-negative cancellation under an even nonlinearity.
Calling square-and-sum invariant to every transformation; it is only approximately invariant to phase rotations within the covered subspace.

modules.title: Task Optimization and Neural Predictivity Are Two Different Tests
modules.guidingQuestion: How can we test whether the internal feature space of a network trained for object classification genuinely resembles a neural representation?
paragraphs: The logic on page 3 spans two data domains. A network first learns weights from a task dataset and classification loss; its feature hierarchy reflects both task and architecture. Freeze the network, compute layer features \(z(x)\) for experimental stimuli, and fit a constrained mapping from z to response r using training neural trials—for example, a ridge-regularized linear readout. Report predictive correlation or explained variance only on held-out stimuli or trials.

High task accuracy does not define neural similarity. Many internal coordinate systems can implement the same classification boundary; networks that rely on texture or shape may score similarly on labels. Predictivity also depends on mapping flexibility. A nonlinear mapper with far more parameters than observations can fit almost any representation to training responses. Use simple mappings of equal complexity and identical cross-validation for every candidate layer.

Let feature matrix \(Z\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times d}\) contain one stimulus per row and one model feature per column, and neural matrix \(R\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times m}\) contain one neuron per column. Fit \(B\in \mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\) by minimizing \(||ZB-R||^{2}\). B aligns coordinate systems but does not change the task representation of the original network. Compare models with the same N, neurons, noise ceiling, and regularization-selection rule.

Neural data contain trial noise, so single-trial correlation cannot reach 1 even when a model captures all reproducible stimulus-driven signal. A noise ceiling estimated from split-half reliability approximates the predictable limit. Report uncertainty with raw and ceiling-normalized predictivity. If one layer scores higher, the justified claim is limited to the current stimuli, area, mapping family, and measurement noise—not mechanistic equivalence to the whole visual system.
keyPoints: Task training determines the representation; a neural readout and held-out evaluation test its alignment with biological responses.
Classification performance and neural predictivity answer different questions and must be reported separately.
Mapping complexity, data splits, and the noise ceiling materially affect the comparison.

derivation.title: Deriving a Neural Readout from a Least-Squares Objective
derivation.setup: For a simple derivation without regularization, choose B to minimize \(L(B)=||ZB-R||_F^{2}\) for model features Z and neural responses R.

steps.title: Write the Matrix Gradient
steps.explanation: The Frobenius norm sums every squared prediction error. Differentiation with respect to B gives twice \(Z^\mathrm{T}\) times the residual.

steps.title: Set the Gradient to Zero
steps.explanation: At the minimum, the normal equation holds, making every feature uncorrelated with the residual.

steps.title: Solve Under Invertibility
steps.explanation: If \(Z^\mathrm{T}Z\) is invertible, left multiplication by its inverse yields the closed-form readout. With collinearity or high dimension, use ridge regularization rather than forcing an inverse.

symbolNotes: N is the number of stimuli, d the number of features, and m the number of neurons. Each column of B contains the readout weights for one neuron.
Estimate B only on the training neural set. If held-out responses influence layer or hyperparameter selection, they no longer constitute an independent test.
derivation.unitsCheck: The units of Z depend on network activations. B has neural-response-units per feature-unit so that ZB and R both use spikes/s or trial counts.
derivation.limitCheck: With only a constant column in Z, the model predicts only each neuron's mean response. If \(d\ge N\) without regularization, training error may be tiny while overfitting is severe.

workedExample.title: A Least-Squares Readout from One Feature
workedExample.problem: For three training stimuli, the model feature is \(z=[1,2,3]\) and one neuron's responses are \(r=[2,4,5]\). Without an intercept, find scalar weight b and predict the response at \(z=4\).
steps: The one-dimensional normal equation gives \(b=(z^\mathrm{T} r)/(z^\mathrm{T} z)\).
\(z^\mathrm{T} r=1\times 2+2\times 4+3\times 5=25\) and \(z^\mathrm{T}z=1+4+9=14\), so \(b=25/14\approx 1.786\).
For a new stimulus with \(z=4\), prediction is \(4b=100/14\approx 7.14\). Its reliability must be tested against the actual held-out response.
workedExample.result: Training data give \(b\approx 1.786\), and held-out feature 4 maps to \(\mathrm{prediction}\approx 7.14\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: If \(r=2z\) exactly, the formula returns \(b=2\). Here the third point is below 6, so the fitted slope is slightly below 2.

selfCheck.prompt: Why is it invalid to repeatedly select the most brain-like network layer on test neural stimuli and report its highest correlation on the same data?
selfCheck.answer: Repeated layer selection already uses the test responses. The maximum contains positive selection noise and is biased upward. Choose layers and regularization on validation neural data and perform the final evaluation once on an independent test set.

pitfalls: Mistaking the fitting power of a flexible nonlinear mapping for similarity between the original representation and neural representation.
Comparing raw correlations across datasets without accounting for neural-response reliability.

modules.title: E/I Recurrence, Nullclines, and Inhibition Stabilization
modules.guidingQuestion: How can a fixed-point shift produce surround suppression, and why might inhibitory-population firing decrease?
paragraphs: Page 4 places surround effects in an E/I recurrent rate model. One common form is \(\tau _{E} dr_{E}/dt=-r_{E}+F_{E}(w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E})\) and \(\tau _{I} dr_{I}/dt=-r_{I}+F_{I}(w_{\mathrm{IE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{II}} r_{I}+I_{I})\). The weights are positive magnitudes and inhibition already carries a minus sign. Recurrent excitation, feedback inhibition, and external inputs jointly determine the fixed point. One population's firing rate is not identical to the net current it delivers to a target.

Within a piecewise-linear region, temporarily set F to identity. The E-nullcline is \(r_{E}=w_{\mathrm{EE}} r_{E}-w_{\mathrm{EI}} r_{I}+I_{E}\), and the I-nullcline can also be rearranged as a line giving \(r_{I}\) versus \(r_{E}\). Their intersection is the steady state. If surround increases external drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population, it shifts the I-nullcline. In an ISN regime, the added drive initially strengthens inhibition and lowers \(r_{E}\), which then reduces recurrent excitation to I. The new intersection can have lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\).

The ISN on page 5 has an excitatory subnetwork that would be unstable in isolation—effective recurrent E gain exceeds leak—but fast inhibitory feedback stabilizes the complete E/I network. The name does not mean that inhibitory firing always rises or that every suppression comes from added I input. Under some perturbations, stronger external drive to I lowers its steady-state rate. This paradoxical response arises from network rebalancing and tests ISN structure more directly than simply measuring whether I is large.

Read a nullcline plot in four steps: label both axes and zero-derivative curves; determine where each derivative is positive; locate intersections; and ask whether arrows after a small displacement return to the intersection. An intersection alone does not establish stability. With nonlinear F there may be several intersections, and surround can change gain instead of only shifting input. The linear example exposes causal structure, while realistic fitting must retain nonlinearities and temporal dynamics.
keyPoints: Surround suppression is a shift of the full recurrent fixed point and does not require an increase in inhibitory firing rate.
Nullcline intersections give steady states; local vector fields or Jacobian eigenvalues determine stability.
An ISN has an unstable E-only subsystem but a stable complete E/I loop; it is not merely a network with qualitatively strong inhibition.

derivation.title: Fixed Point, Surround Shift, and Local Stability in a Linear E/I Network
derivation.setup: Within the current operating range, set \(F_{E}\) and \(F_{I}\) to identity, use one positive time constant \(\tau\) for both populations, and choose \(w_{\mathrm{EE}}=1.2\), \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}=1\), \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}=1\), \(w_{\mathrm{II}}=0\). The fixed-point equations are \(0=-r_{E}+1.2r_{E}-r_{I}+I_{E}\) and \(0=-r_{I}+r_{E}+I_{I}\).

steps.title: Express \(r_{I}\) from the I Equation
steps.explanation: The second fixed-point equation directly gives \(r_{I}=r_{E}+I_{I}\); substitute it into the E equation.

steps.title: Solve for \(r_{E}\)
steps.explanation: The E equation becomes \(0.2r_{E}-r_{I}+I_{E}=0\). After substitution and rearrangement, \(0.8r_{E}=I_{E}-I_{I}\).

steps.title: Recover \(r_{I}\) and Compare Conditions
steps.explanation: Compute the new intersection from \(r_{E}\) and then use \(r_{I}=r_{E}+I_{I}\). Both rates can fall when surround input changes.

steps.title: Verify the ISN Conditions with the Jacobian
steps.explanation: The full E/I linearization is \((1/\tau )[[0.2,-1],[1,-1]]\), whose eigenvalues are \((-0.4\pm 0.8i)/\tau\). Their real parts are negative, so the intersection is locally stable. Removing inhibitory feedback leaves E-only eigenvalue \(0.2/\tau >0\), making the isolated E subsystem unstable. These two results—not nullcline intersection by itself—establish that the example is an ISN.

symbolNotes: \(w_{\mathrm{EE}}=1.2\) exceeds unit leak, so the linear E-only subsystem grows. Stability of the full system also depends on inhibitory feedback and time constants.
Identity F applies only locally where rates are positive and unsaturated. A negative calculated rate requires rectification and a new active-set analysis.
derivation.unitsCheck: For rates in spikes/s, dimensionless weights map presynaptic rates into drive of the same units, and \(I_{E}\),\(I_{I}\) are equivalent rate drives. Jacobian eigenvalues contain \(1/\tau\) and therefore have reciprocal-time units.
derivation.limitCheck: Setting \(w_{\mathrm{EI}}\) or \(w_{\mathrm{IE}}\) to zero breaks the stabilizing E/I feedback loop. If E gain exceeds leak, the E-only mode runs away, exposing the ISN condition.

workedExample.title: Surround Suppression with Simultaneous Decreases in E and I Rates
workedExample.problem: Use the derived network. For center only, \(I_{E}=10\) and \(I_{I}=2\). With surround, \(I_{E}\) remains 10 but drive \(I_{I}\) to the inhibitory population rises to 5. Find both fixed points.
steps: Thus E falls from 10 to 6.25 and I from 12 to 11.25. Although the I population receives more external drive, its steady rate falls slightly because recurrent E input falls more.
workedExample.result: Both steady-state E and I are lower with surround; this does not exclude a role for recurrent inhibition.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Substitution verifies the surround E equation: \(-6.25+1.2\times 6.25-11.25+10=0\); and I equation: \(-11.25+6.25+5=0\).

selfCheck.prompt: Why does lower inhibitory-neuron firing after surround not imply that inhibition did not cause surround suppression?
selfCheck.answer: A firing rate is the network fixed-point outcome, while inhibitory current also depends on connectivity and presynaptic rate. Surround can first lower E drive and thereby lower I, even though I feedback still determines the fixed point at which E amplification is contained.

pitfalls: Conflating inhibitory-population rate, inhibitory current received by a target, and net suppression.
Declaring an intersection stable from the nullclines alone without inspecting the local vector field or Jacobian eigenvalues.

objectives: Draw the brain, body, and environment as a closed-loop dynamical system and distinguish feedforward commands, sensory feedback, state estimates, and external disturbances.
Generalize the first-order equation for one neuron to \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), correctly interpreting the direction of \(W_{ij}\) and every matrix shape.
When W is diagonalizable, transform population activity into its eigenbasis and derive mutually decoupled mode equations step by step.
From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability.
Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback.
prerequisiteBridge: First review scalar system \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+u\). Without input, -h returns the state toward zero. Constant u shifts the fixed point to \(h^{*}=u\), and the solution decays as \(e^{-t/\tau }\). Feedback makes input depend on state, for example \(u=\lambda h+I\), changing the restoring coefficient from 1 to \(1-\lambda\). A recurrent population replaces scalar h by a vector and \(\lambda\) by matrix W; every eigenmode repeats the same scalar logic.

Fix the convention for W before calculation. Here \((Wh)_i=\sum _j W_{ij} h_{j}\), so \(W_{ij}\) is the effect of population j on population i: the column is source and the row is target. \(h\in \mathbb{R}^N\) is an N-unit activity column vector and \(W\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\). An eigenvector v satisfies \(Wv=\lambda v\), meaning a recurrent multiplication preserves the population pattern's direction and scales it by \(\lambda\).

Diagonalization \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\) requires N linearly independent eigenvectors. The columns of V are \(v_{i}\) and the diagonal entries of \(\Lambda\) are \(\lambda _{i}\). Writing \(h=V\alpha\) gives mode amplitudes \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), not another population of real neurons. An asymmetric W can have complex eigenvalues or be defective. Dynamics remain valid but require real oscillatory blocks, generalized eigenvectors, or the matrix exponential directly. The course first treats the diagonalizable case to expose timescale and stability clearly.

diagnostic.prompt: Under convention \((Wh)_i=\sum _j W_{ij}h_{j}\), does \(W_{ij}\) represent a connection from i to j or from j to i?
diagnostic.answer: It represents source j to target i, because \(W_{ij}h_{j}\) contributes to output component i.
diagnostic.explanation: Some texts use the transposed convention. Expanding the matrix multiplication first prevents reversing the connection diagram.

diagnostic.prompt: If \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\) and an eigenvalue \(\lambda =0\), what is the mode's effective time constant?
diagnostic.answer: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )=20 \mathrm{ms}\), equal to the intrinsic time constant without recurrent feedback.
diagnostic.explanation: \(\lambda =0\) means no recurrent input along that mode, so leak alone sets decay.

diagnostic.prompt: Which continuous-time mode decays more slowly, \(\lambda =0.9\) or \(\lambda =-0.5\)?
diagnostic.answer: \(\lambda =0.9\) is slower, with \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=10\tau\); \(\lambda =-0.5\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /1.5\), so negative feedback accelerates decay beyond the intrinsic rate.
diagnostic.explanation: For this continuous-time equation, the stability boundary for a real eigenvalue is 1, not absolute value 1, because the dynamics contain -I+W.

diagnostic.prompt: Is eigenmode amplitude \(\alpha _{i}\) the firing rate of neuron i?
diagnostic.answer: Usually not. \(\alpha _{i}\) is the coordinate of the population vector along eigenvector \(v_{i}\), and one mode generally combines many neurons.
diagnostic.explanation: A mode coincides with one neuron coordinate only when W is diagonal in the neuronal basis. Treating modes as neurons misreads distributed dynamics.

modules.title: Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop
modules.guidingQuestion: Why is a single command arrow from motor cortex to muscle insufficient to explain stability and correction during real movement?
paragraphs: Page 1 embeds the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup.

A feedforward command acts in advance from a goal and internal model and can compensate for known delays, but it is vulnerable to unexpected disturbances and model error. A feedback controller corrects output using sensed state error and resists disturbances, but excessive gain combined with delay can oscillate. Biological control combines both, with spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and motor cortex contributing on different timescales and representational levels rather than taking over sequentially.

A sensory signal is a delayed noisy observation, not the body's exact current state. A state estimate combines recent sensation, copies of motor commands, and a dynamics model to infer current latent position, velocity, and related variables. Feedback commonly computes error around this estimate. A central pattern generator (CPG) shows that a recurrent circuit can generate rhythmic motor output without an external command on every cycle; sensory feedback corrects phase and amplitude rather than generating each cycle from scratch.

A minimal scalar example writes body position dynamics as \(dx/dt=u+d\), with neural command u and external disturbance d. Proportional feedback \(u=-kx\) gives \(dx/dt=-kx+d\). Without persistent disturbance, x returns to zero at rate k. Under constant disturbance, fixed error is d/k. Raising k reduces steady error, but sensory delay, actuator limits, and noise constrain gain in real systems, foreshadowing recurrent-stability tradeoffs.

Distributed motor-cortical activity need not map one neuron to one muscle. A movement can be represented by a population trajectory: instantaneous activity is the dynamical state, and recurrent dynamics determine how the trajectory continues. The question expands from which neuron encodes which variable to which modes govern population-state evolution and which inputs alter initial conditions or the vector field. A linear network is not a complete motor theory, but it is the first decomposition of temporal structure.
keyPoints: Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback.
Feedforward control anticipates; feedback corrects disturbances. Delay, noise, and gain set the stability costs.
A state estimate infers current latent state from delayed noisy observations, while a CPG demonstrates endogenous rhythm generation by recurrent dynamics.
Motor-population activity is a dynamical state; no mode should be assumed to equal one muscle or action variable.

derivation.title: How Proportional Feedback Rejects a Constant Disturbance
derivation.setup: Use normalized one-dimensional body dynamics \(dx/dt=u+d\) with target position 0 and proportional controller \(u=-kx\), where \(k>0\).

steps.title: Substitute the Feedback Law
steps.explanation: The controller converts positive position error into a negative command, yielding a first-order equation with constant forcing.

steps.title: Find the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: At steady state the derivative vanishes, so restoring command kx* balances disturbance d.

steps.title: Find Dynamics Relative to the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Set \(e=x-x^{*}\). Constant terms cancel after substitution, and error decays as \(e^{-kt}\).

symbolNotes: k is feedback gain and has inverse-time units in this normalized equation.
d is written as a position-velocity disturbance. Mechanics with mass would change the units and state dimension.
derivation.unitsCheck: x has position units and \(dx/dt\), u, and d have position/time units. Thus kx has position/time units and k has units 1/time.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(k\to 0\), restoring feedback disappears and constant disturbance makes position drift. Increasing k reduces ideal-model error, but an unmodeled delay can destabilize high gain.

workedExample.title: Steady Position Error Under a Persistent Velocity Disturbance
workedExample.problem: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\).
steps: The fixed point is \(x^{*}=d/k=0.6/2=0.3\).
Error \(e=x-0.3\) obeys \(de/dt=-2e\), so \(e(t)=0.7e^{-2t}\) and the time constant is 1/2 s.
workedExample.result: The system converges not to zero but to steady error 0.3; at 1 second its position is about 0.395.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At initial \(x=1\), derivative=\(-2+0.6=-1.4\), so the trajectory must move downward. The computed result has the correct direction.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does larger proportional gain improve disturbance rejection in a delay-free model but not justify infinite gain in a biological system?
selfCheck.answer: The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop.

pitfalls: Treating feedforward and feedback as mutually exclusive, although real actions commonly combine predictive commands with sensory correction.
Assigning one function to each motor region from a region list while ignoring circuits, parallel pathways, and the abstraction level of the course diagram.

modules.title: The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition
modules.guidingQuestion: How can N coupled rate equations be rewritten as independent scalar equations, one for each eigenmode?
paragraphs: Page 2 begins with \(\tau  dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\). Vector \(h\in \mathbb{R}^N\) contains the activities of N units, -h is unitwise leak, Wh is recurrent input, and I is external drive. Here \(W_{ij}\) points from j to i. In neuronal coordinates, each derivative depends on many \(h_{j}\) and the equations are coupled. We seek coordinates in which recurrent multiplication no longer mixes components.

Page 3 uses right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates.

Substitute \(h=V\alpha\) into the original equation and take V to be time-independent: \(\tau V d\alpha /dt=-V\alpha +WV\alpha +I\). Using \(WV=V\Lambda\) and left-multiplying by \(V^{-1}\) gives \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-\alpha +\Lambda \alpha +V^{-1}I\). Since \(\Lambda\) is diagonal, row i contains only \(\alpha _{i}\): \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). The complex network's linear dynamics decompose into familiar first-order systems.

The limitations matter. Eigenvectors of asymmetric W need not be orthogonal, so \(V^{-1}\) cannot be replaced casually by \(V^\mathrm{T}\). Nearly parallel eigenvectors make mode coordinates noise-sensitive. If W is defective, there is no complete ordinary eigenbasis; use Jordan form or \(e^{(-I+W)t/\tau }\) directly. The diagonalizable case highlights eigenvalue control of timescale but does not claim that cortical connectivity is symmetric.
keyPoints: The direction of \(W_{ij}\) follows by expanding \((Wh)_i\); here it is \(j\to i\).
\(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns.
When W is diagonalizable, \(\Lambda\) does not mix modes and every \(\alpha _{i}\) follows an independent first-order equation.

derivation.title: From the Recurrent Equation to Decoupled Mode Equations
derivation.setup: Assume W has a complete eigenvector matrix V with \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Let \(h=V\alpha\) and define transformed input \(\widetilde I=V^{-1}I\).

steps.title: Substitute the Activity Expansion
steps.explanation: V is constant, so \(dh/dt=Vd\alpha /dt\). Replace each occurrence of h by \(V\alpha\).

steps.title: Use the Eigenvector Relation
steps.explanation: \(WV=V\Lambda\) because every column of V is an eigenvector of W.

steps.title: Left-Multiply by the Inverse Basis
steps.explanation: Left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\) removes V and projects external input into mode coordinates.

steps.title: Read the ith Diagonal Equation
steps.explanation: Only diagonal entry \(\lambda _{i}\) appears in row i of \(\Lambda\), so derivative i no longer contains another \(\alpha _{j}\).

symbolNotes: The columns of V are right eigenvectors; rows of \(V^{-1}\) read the coordinates \(\alpha\).
Ĩ_i is the input component in a left-eigenvector coordinate, not necessarily a simple Euclidean dot product.
derivation.unitsCheck: If V consists of dimensionless normalized patterns, \(\alpha\) and h have firing-rate units; W and \(\lambda\) are dimensionless, \(\tau\) has time units, and Ĩ has the same units as h.
derivation.limitCheck: For \(W=0\), choose \(V=I\) and \(\lambda _{i}=0\); every neuronal mode decays independently with \(\tau\). If W is already diagonal, the basis change leaves the coordinates unchanged.

workedExample.title: Common and Difference Modes in a Two-Neuron Network
workedExample.problem: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations.
steps: For difference pattern \(v_{-}=(1,-1)/\sqrt 2\), \(Wv_{-}=(0.7,-0.7)/\sqrt 2\), so \(\lambda _{-}=0.7\).
The mode equations are \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{+}/dt=-0.1\alpha _{+}\) and \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{-}/dt=-0.3\alpha _{-}\). The common mode decays more slowly.
workedExample.result: Population activity decomposes into an aligned common mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and an opposing difference mode with \(\lambda =0.7\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: Matrix \(\operatorname{trace} 1.6\) equals eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 0.9+0.7\), and determinant 0.63 equals product \(0.9\times 0.7\).

selfCheck.prompt: For asymmetric W, why can normalized right eigenvectors not justify writing \(\alpha =V^\mathrm{T} h\)?
selfCheck.answer: Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes.

pitfalls: Inferring source-target direction of \(W_{ij}\) by habit instead of expanding the matrix product.
Assuming every W has an orthonormal eigenbasis, a property restricted to special matrices such as real symmetric ones.

modules.title: Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration
modules.guidingQuestion: Why does \(\lambda\) near 1 create long memory, while \(\lambda =1\) and \(\lambda >1 \operatorname{mean}\) perfect integration and instability?
paragraphs: Page 4 begins with input-free equation \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}\). For real \(\lambda _{i}<1\), \(\alpha _{i}(t)=\alpha _{i}(0)\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})t/\tau ]\), giving \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\). Positive recurrent feedback pushes \(\lambda\) toward 1, offsets leak, and lengthens memory; negative \(\lambda\) strengthens restoration and accelerates decay. Continuous-time stability requires Re(λ_i)<1, not \(|\lambda _{i}|<1\).

At \(\lambda _{i}=1\), restoring force vanishes. Without input \(\alpha _{i}\) holds its initial value; with time-varying input, \(\tau  d\alpha _{i}/dt=\widetilde I_{i}(t)\), so the state accumulates the input integral—a perfect integrator. For \(\lambda _{i}\) slightly below 1 there is long but finite leakage; for \(\lambda _{i}>1\) small perturbations grow exponentially. Under constant input, algebraic fixed point \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\) may still exist, but it is unstable: any initial condition not exactly at that point departs. Nonlinear saturation may create another attractor, beyond the local range of this linear mode.

Page 5 also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity.

For arbitrary time-varying input, the mode response is the sum of decaying initial condition and input convolution. Kernel \(\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})(t-s)/\tau ]/\tau\) weights only past input. As \(\lambda _{i}\) approaches 1, the kernel decays more slowly and older inputs continue to influence present state. The impulse response therefore exposes \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) directly, while transformed-input magnitude \(\widetilde I_{i}=V^{-1}I\) determines whether external drive enters that slow mode.

In population space, \(h(t)=V\alpha (t)\) sums all modal time courses. A slow mode may dominate the late trajectory even with a small initial projection because faster modes vanish first. An input's effect depends on which modes it projects onto, not only its total energy. An eigenvalue account of motor dynamics should report model fit, initial conditions, input projection, and observed timescale; a rotating trajectory alone does not identify an eigenmode as a behavioral command.
keyPoints: For a real eigenvalue \(\lambda <1\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); decay slows as the eigenvalue approaches 1.
\(\lambda =1\) removes leak and integrates input; \(\lambda >1\) makes the linear mode grow exponentially.
Approaching 1 increases both memory time and constant-input gain, amplifying bias and connectivity error as well.

derivation.title: Mode Solution, Effective Time Constant, and Fixed Point
derivation.setup: Consider one real mode \(\tau  d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha +\widetilde I\), initially with constant input.

steps.title: Find the Constant-Input Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Set the derivative to zero and solve for \(\alpha\)* when \(\lambda \ne 1\).

steps.title: Rewrite Error Relative to the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Let \(e=\alpha -\alpha *\). Constant input and fixed-point terms cancel, leaving a homogeneous equation.

steps.title: Integrate the Homogeneous Equation
steps.explanation: Separate de/e from dt, integrate to obtain the exponential solution, and express its coefficient as an effective time constant.

steps.title: Extend to Time-Varying Input
steps.explanation: Use an integrating factor to retain the initial-condition term and weight transformed input at every past time s by the exponential impulse response. This convolution shows that a mode is a leaky temporal filter.

steps.title: Handle \(\lambda =1\) Separately
steps.explanation: The fixed-point formula containing \(1-\lambda\) cannot be used. The equation becomes derivative equal to input divided by \(\tau\).

symbolNotes: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) is a positive decay time only for a stable real mode \(\lambda <1\). For \(\lambda >1\), use growth time \(\tau /(\lambda -1)\).
A complex \(\lambda\) produces oscillations set by its imaginary part, while 1-Re(λ) determines envelope stability.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\lambda\) is dimensionless, while \(\tau\) and \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) are times. \(\alpha\) and Ĩ share units, so \(\int \widetilde I ds/\tau\) retains the units of \(\alpha\).
derivation.limitCheck: \(\lambda =0\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, both \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and constant gain grow. For \(\lambda >1\), the exponent changes sign and the zero fixed point is unstable.

workedExample.title: Extending an Intrinsic 20 ms Time Constant to 1 s of Memory
workedExample.problem: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\).
steps: Because \(1-\lambda =0.02\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20 \mathrm{ms}/0.02=1000 \mathrm{ms}=1 \mathrm{s}\).
After 1 s, \(\alpha =5e^{-1}\approx 1.84\). Recurrent feedback lengthens but does not eliminate decay.
For \(\lambda =1\) without input, \(d\alpha /dt=0\) and the amplitude remains 5 after 1 s. A persistent small bias would be integrated continuously.
workedExample.result: \(\lambda =0.98\) turns an intrinsic 20 ms constant into a 1 s leaky memory; only \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The incorrect formula \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1+\lambda )\) gives about 10 ms, the opposite of the memory-lengthening effect of positive feedback.

selfCheck.prompt: Why does changing \(\lambda\) from 0.98 to 0.999 create drift risk in addition to longer memory?
selfCheck.answer: The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement.

pitfalls: Applying the discrete-time condition \(|\lambda |<1\) directly to continuous-time equation \(\tau dh/dt=(-I+W)h\).
Continuing to use \(\alpha *=\widetilde I/(1-\lambda )\) at \(\lambda =1\), despite a perfect integrator having no finite fixed point under constant input.
